canonical_answers.title: Pump Selection for Ship's Services
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Bilge pumping**
Reciprocating (positive-displacement) pump — self-priming with a good suction lift, so it can draw from a low or partly dry bilge and handle dirty, solids-laden water.
Centrifugal pump (with priming aid) — moves large volumes for rapid dewatering; robust and simple, and with an open/non-clog impeller can pass small debris.

**(b) Lubricating oil circulating**
Screw pump — gives smooth, pulsation-free delivery ideal for viscous oil and maintains steady pressure to the bearings.
Gear pump — positive displacement provides constant delivery against system resistance and copes well with high L.O. viscosity.

**(c) Sea water circulating**
Centrifugal pump — suited to large volumes of low-viscosity water at the low/moderate heads of cooling circuits; reliable for continuous duty.
Axial-flow (propeller) pump — delivers very high flow at low head, well matched to large SW circulating duties such as condenser/cooler cooling.

**(d) Sewage sludge**
Progressive cavity (mono) pump — handles thick, viscous, solids-laden sludge with a gentle, non-clogging action and steady delivery.
Diaphragm pump — self-priming, tolerates abrasive/stringy solids and dry running, with no fine clearances to jam. (A non-clog/vortex-impeller centrifugal is an acceptable alternative.)

**(e) Steering gear**
Variable-delivery axial-piston pump (swash-plate) — gives infinitely variable, reversible flow for proportional rudder control at the high pressures the rams need.
Variable-delivery radial-piston pump (Hele-Shaw) — provides variable, reversible delivery from a constant-speed motor, suited to the high-pressure hydraulic steering circuit.

**Logic:** match positive-displacement pumps to viscous, self-priming, suction-lift or high-pressure duties (L.O., sludge, steering, bilge suction); match centrifugal/axial pumps to high-volume, low-viscosity duties (SW circulating, bulk bilge dewatering).
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged yet for this occurrence, but the mark-earning logic is matching pump type to duty: positive-displacement pumps (reciprocating, screw, gear, diaphragm, axial-piston) suit viscous, self-priming, suction-lift or high-pressure duties (L.O., sludge, steering, bilge suction); centrifugal/axial pumps suit high-volume, low-viscosity duties (SW circulating, bulk bilge dewatering).

canonical_answers.title: Double-Entry Impeller; Two-Speed vs Throttling
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Double-entry (double-suction) impeller — sketch**
*Sketch instructions: draw a horizontal shaft with a central boss. On both sides of the boss draw a curved impeller eye (suction inlet). Show arrows entering axially from left and right into the two eyes, turning 90° inside the impeller, then discharging radially outward at the outer diameter into the volute casing. Label: Suction inlet (both sides), Shaft, Impeller vanes, Discharge (radial) to volute.*
Water enters the impeller axially from both ends (one suction eye on each side of the shaft), turns through 90° inside the impeller, and is discharged radially at the outer diameter into the common volute.

**(b) Why double-entry impellers are fitted**
The dominant reason is **axial-thrust balance**: the two eyes face in opposite directions, so the axial forces cancel and the thrust bearing is relieved. Splitting the flow into two halves also lowers the inlet velocity and the NPSH required, reducing cavitation risk and allowing a higher total capacity — suited to large-throughput duties such as main sea-water circulating.

**(c) Two-speed operation versus throttling**
A centrifugal pump's duty is set by where its characteristic curve meets the system resistance curve (friction head, which rises roughly with flow squared). A lower flow can be obtained either by throttling a valve or by reducing pump speed.

*Head/Flow diagram: at full speed (curve N1) the pump runs at point A (high capacity). Throttling partly closes the discharge valve, steepening the system curve, so the duty slides up curve N1 to point B: low flow but still high head — the surplus head between B and what the pipework actually needs (point C) is dropped across the valve and wasted as heat, while the pump keeps absorbing nearly full power. Reducing speed drops the whole pump curve to N2, meeting the original system curve at point C — the same low flow at a much lower head.*

By the affinity laws Q ∝ N, H ∝ N² and crucially P ∝ N³, so halving the speed cuts power to about an eighth. For a large SW circulating pump whose demand swings between high capacity (full power / warm water) and low capacity (part load / cold water), the cube-law power saving makes two-speed operation clearly preferable to wasting power continuously across a throttle valve. The only limitation is that two fixed speeds give two operating points rather than infinite control — adequate for a two-level cooling duty.
examiner_focus: The sketch is the main mark-loser -- candidates repeatedly draw a multi-stage arrangement instead of a double-suction (double-entry) impeller, and few mention axial-thrust balance in part (b), which is the actual reason for fitting one.

canonical_answers.title: Impeller & Volute Function; Impeller Features
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) The impeller**
The impeller is the rotating element that puts energy into the liquid. Liquid enters at the eye and is flung outward by the curved vanes; the rotation accelerates it, raising its velocity (kinetic energy) and giving it centrifugal head. It converts the mechanical energy of the shaft into kinetic energy in the fluid, delivered at high velocity to the impeller periphery.

**(a)(ii) The volute**
The volute is the spiral casing passage surrounding the impeller, of increasing cross-section toward the discharge. As the high-velocity liquid passes through this expanding passage its velocity falls and, by Bernoulli, kinetic energy is converted into pressure energy. The volute therefore turns velocity head into useful pressure head while collecting and guiding the flow to the outlet.

**(b)(i) A double-entry impeller**
Chiefly to balance axial thrust (the two eyes face opposite ways so axial forces cancel). It also splits the flow, lowering inlet velocity and NPSH required and allowing higher capacity — e.g. main sea-water circulating.

**(b)(ii) A diffuser ring**
A ring of fixed guide vanes around the impeller forming gradually widening passages. It converts velocity to pressure more efficiently and uniformly than a plain volute, recovers more head, and by guiding the flow symmetrically gives balanced radial pressure (reducing radial thrust). Typical of high-head and multi-stage pumps.

**(b)(iii) More than one impeller (multi-staging)**
To develop a high total head a single impeller could not. Impellers in series on one shaft each feed the next, so the heads add together, giving high delivery pressure (e.g. boiler feed) while keeping each impeller's diameter, tip speed and stress at efficient values.
examiner_focus: Candidates confuse the diffuser ring with a sacrificial wear ring, describing it as something that wears away rather than a fixed ring of guide vanes that converts velocity to pressure.

canonical_answers.title: Gear-Type Pump — Principle, Materials, Application
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Principle of operation**
A gear pump is a positive-displacement pump. Two close-meshing gears — a driving gear and a driven (idler) gear — run in a casing with very small tip and end clearances. On the suction side the teeth continuously come out of mesh, so the enclosed space increases and a partial vacuum draws liquid in. The liquid is trapped in the pockets between the teeth and the casing wall and carried around the outside (periphery) of each gear — not through the centre. On the discharge side the teeth come back into mesh, the volume reduces, and the liquid is positively displaced out under pressure. The line of meshing teeth seals against back-flow. Delivery is near-constant per revolution, so a relief valve is always fitted.
*Sketch instructions: draw two meshing gears side by side in a close-fitting casing. Grey arrows show gear rotation (opposite directions where they mesh); blue arrows trace the liquid path — in at the suction side, around the outer periphery of each gear in the tooth pockets, out at the discharge side. Label suction (in), discharge (out), driving gear, driven/idler gear, and the meshing point where back-flow is sealed.*

**(b) Materials of construction**
Casing/body — cast iron or cast steel for oil duties; bronze or gunmetal for corrosive/seawater service; aluminium for light duty.
Gears — case-hardened alloy steel (most common); cast iron or bronze for lighter/corrosive service; sometimes one non-metallic gear (Tufnol/phenolic) to reduce wear and noise.
Shafts — hardened/alloy steel.
Bushes, bearings, end (wear) plates — bronze, gunmetal or white-metal; needle or ball bearings on some designs.
Shaft seal — mechanical seal or lip seal.

**(c) Suitable application and why**
Lubricating-oil circulating/transfer (equally fuel-oil and hydraulic duties). As positive-displacement units they deliver a steady, near-constant volume against varying back-pressure (keeping bearing oil pressure stable), are self-priming, give relatively smooth low-pulsation delivery, handle viscous oils well and can develop the high pressures required, while remaining compact, simple and reliable.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the sketch trap to watch for is showing liquid flowing through the centre of the meshing gears rather than around the outer periphery of each gear in the tooth pockets.

canonical_answers.title: Operating Principle; NPSHa Definition & Temperature Effects
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Operating principle**
Liquid enters axially at the eye of a rotating impeller. The curved vanes fling it radially outward and accelerate it, so it leaves the periphery at high velocity (kinetic energy). It then passes into the volute or diffuser — a passage of increasing area — where the velocity falls and that kinetic energy is converted into pressure energy, delivering the liquid at a useful outlet pressure. Continuous removal of liquid from the eye keeps the pressure there low, drawing in fresh liquid and maintaining steady flow. As it relies on imparting velocity, it is not self-priming and its delivery varies with the head against which it works.

**(b) NPSH available (NPSHa)**
NPSHa is the total suction head actually available at the impeller eye above the vapour pressure of the liquid, expressed as a head of that liquid — the margin of pressure energy at the suction over the liquid's vapour pressure that prevents it flashing into vapour as it enters the impeller. For cavitation-free running, NPSHa must exceed the pump's NPSH required (NPSHr).
NPSHa = absolute pressure head at the surface ± static suction head − suction-line friction losses − vapour-pressure head of the liquid.

**(c) Effect of temperature on NPSHa**
Raising the liquid temperature raises its vapour pressure. Since vapour-pressure head is subtracted, higher temperature reduces NPSHa (less margin above boiling) and increases cavitation risk — why hot-well, condensate and feed suctions are prone to cavitation. (A slight fall in density is a minor secondary effect; the rise in vapour pressure dominates.)

**(d) Overcoming the temperature effect**
Provide a positive (flooded) suction head — pump below the source, or tank raised; feed deaerator/hot-well mounted high above the feed pump.
Pressurise the suction source to raise the absolute pressure head at the surface.
Reduce suction-line losses — short, large-bore, smooth piping with minimal bends/fittings.
Reduce suction velocity / NPSHr — low-speed or double-entry first stage, or a booster pump.
Where possible, limit or sub-cool the suction temperature to lower the vapour pressure.
examiner_focus: NPSHa is poorly understood across sittings even though it recurs frequently: candidates rarely link temperature to vapour pressure in part (c), and a common wrong answer for 'how the effects of temperature are overcome' in part (d) is simply 'fit a cooler' -- the fix is reducing suction losses/lift or raising suction head, not cooling the liquid.

canonical_answers.title: NPSHa versus NPSHr; Increasing NPSHa by Design
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) NPSHa versus NPSHr**
NPSHa (available) is set by the system — the suction head actually delivered to the impeller eye above the liquid's vapour pressure (atmospheric/tank pressure ± static suction head − suction friction losses − vapour-pressure head). Friction losses grow with flow squared, so NPSHa falls as flow increases.
NPSHr (required) is set by the pump, fixed by its design and speed. As liquid accelerates into the eye its pressure drops below the flange value; NPSHr is the minimum margin above vapour pressure needed at the flange so the liquid does not flash at the lowest internal point. Entry losses rise with velocity, so NPSHr increases with flow (roughly with Q²).

*Diagram: plot NPSH (y-axis) against flow rate Q (x-axis). NPSHa is a curve falling as Q rises; NPSHr is a curve rising as Q rises. To the left of where the two curves cross, NPSHa > NPSHr (safe, no cavitation); to the right, NPSHr > NPSHa (cavitation). The crossing point marks the limiting flow.*

The rule is NPSHa > NPSHr (with a margin). To the left of the crossing the pump is safe; at the crossing they are equal — the limiting flow; to the right NPSHr exceeds NPSHa and the pump cavitates (loss of head, noise, vibration, impeller erosion). NPSHa is what the installation supplies; NPSHr is what the pump demands.

**(b) Increasing NPSHa by design**
Provide a positive (flooded) suction head — pump below the supply, or the tank raised (e.g. feed deaerator high above the feed pump).
Pressurise the suction vessel to raise the absolute pressure head on the surface.
Reduce suction-line losses — short, large-bore, smooth piping, few bends/fittings, full-bore valves.
Fit a booster pump on the suction.
Keep the suction temperature down (or slightly sub-cool) to lower the vapour pressure.
examiner_focus: The NPSHa-vs-NPSHr diagram is weakly answered across sittings -- sketches tend to be vague rather than clearly showing the margin between the two curves that defines the safety margin against cavitation.

canonical_answers.title: Principle & Relief Valve; Double Entry; Routine Overhaul
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Principle and why no relief valve is needed**
The impeller imparts velocity (kinetic) energy to the liquid, which is then converted into pressure energy in the volute/diffuser. A relief valve is unnecessary because the pump can only develop its fixed shut-off (maximum) head: if the discharge is closed or blocked the impeller merely churns the trapped liquid and the pressure rises no higher. Unlike a positive-displacement pump (which keeps displacing a fixed volume and would build dangerous pressure), the centrifugal is inherently self-limiting.

**(b) Why a double-entry impeller**
Mainly to balance axial thrust — a suction eye each side gives equal, opposite axial forces that cancel, relieving the thrust bearing. Splitting the flow also lowers inlet velocity and NPSH required, reducing cavitation risk and allowing higher capacity (e.g. main sea-water circulating).

**(c) Routine overhaul**
After isolating the pump electrically and mechanically, shutting the valves and draining it, uncouple the driver, remove the casing/cover and withdraw the rotating assembly; clean and inspect.

**Inspections:**
Impeller — vanes/shrouds for cavitation pitting, erosion, cracks, wear (especially eye and tips).
Wear (neck) rings — casing and impeller rings for wear and scoring (they control internal leakage).
Shaft — wear, scoring, bending, corrosion (under the sleeve and at journals).
Shaft sleeve — grooving/wear where the seal runs.
Casing/volute — erosion, pitting, corrosion.
Bearings — wear, pitting, discolouration, roughness.
Mechanical seal faces (or gland packing) — wear and damage.
Keys, keyways and fasteners — wear and security.

**Measurements:**
Wear-ring clearances — most important; compare with maker's limits (excess clearance causes recirculation and lost head/efficiency).
Shaft straightness/run-out (dial gauge); journal and sleeve diameters.
Shaft end-float/axial position and impeller setting.
On reassembly, coupling alignment (and check for soft foot).

**Likely replacement parts:** wear/neck rings; mechanical seal or gland packing; bearings; all joints, O-rings and gaskets; shaft sleeve; and the impeller or shaft if worn, cracked or badly eroded. Rebuild to correct clearances with new joints/seals, set the rotor, re-align the coupling, then refill, vent and run-test (discharge pressure/flow, leakage, vibration, noise, bearing temperature) before return to service.
examiner_focus: A reliably high-scoring question when it comes up -- the no-relief-valve reasoning (centrifugal delivery isn't positively displaced, so it can't over-pressurise a blocked line) and the double-entry/overhaul detail are usually well known.

canonical_answers.title: Condition Assessment; Misalignment Effects and Correction
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Assessing internal condition without dismantling**
Performance / head check — at known speed, read suction & discharge pressures (developed head) and flow; take motor current/power. A fall in head and flow for the same speed, or a low shut-off pressure, indicates internal wear (enlarged ring clearances, eroded impeller, recirculation).
Vibration analysis — frequency content reveals imbalance/erosion, worn bearings, misalignment and cavitation.
Bearing temperature and noise — high temperature indicates bearing distress; a gravelly rattle with fluctuating gauges indicates cavitation.

**(b) Effects of misalignment**
Heavy vibration, noise and increased power consumption; rapid wear and premature failure of bearings; mechanical seal damage and leakage; coupling wear/fretting; in severe cases shaft fatigue and fracture.

**(c) Correcting misalignment**
Misalignment is either parallel (offset) or angular (often combined). The pump is taken as fixed and the motor moved to suit.
*Sketch instructions: draw the pump (fixed) and motor (movable) connected by a coupling. Show a rim gauge (dial indicator) reading radial/parallel offset, and a face gauge reading angular error. Show shims under the motor feet for vertical/angular correction, and jacking screws at the base for horizontal correction.*

**Prepare:** isolate and lock off; clean feet, baseplate and coupling faces; check holding-down bolts; test for soft foot; set the coupling gap and allow for thermal growth if hot-running.
**Measure:** clamp dial indicators across the coupling (rim and face) or use laser alignment; rotate both shafts together and read at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°. The rim (radial) gauge reveals parallel/offset; the face gauge reveals angular misalignment.
**Correct:** add/remove shims under the motor feet — equal shims for vertical offset, unequal front-to-back to tilt for angular; move the motor sideways with jacking screws for horizontal errors.
**Re-check:** re-read after each adjustment until within tolerance, tighten the bolts and check again (tightening can pull alignment off); on hot units, a final check at running temperature.
examiner_focus: A binary question -- candidates who know the dial-gauge alignment procedure and the effects of misalignment score well, others don't; there's little partial-credit middle ground.

canonical_answers.title: Raising Speed; Multi-Staging; Centrifugal vs PD for L.O.
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Raising the speed of rotation**
A higher speed raises impeller tip velocity, imparting more kinetic energy and head. By the affinity laws flow rises with speed (Q ∝ N) and head with its square (H ∝ N²), so a given impeller develops much greater head and capacity, or the same duty is met by a smaller pump. (Penalty: power rises with the cube of speed, P ∝ N³, and NPSHr increases.)

**(a)(ii) Multi-staging**
Several impellers in series on one shaft, each discharging into the next, so the per-stage heads add up. The total head is roughly the single-stage head times the number of stages while flow stays that of one impeller — giving high delivery pressure (e.g. boiler feed) yet keeping each impeller's diameter, tip speed and stress at efficient values.

**(b) Centrifugal vs PD for L.O. circulating**
No over-pressurisation — limited to shut-off head; a choked filter or closed valve just makes it churn, so no relief valve is needed (a PD pump must have one).
Smooth, pulsation-free delivery — steady oil supply and film to bearings, less pipework fatigue and vibration.
High capacity, compact and simple — large volume at low head efficiently; only the impeller rotates, so smaller, lighter, cheaper and very reliable.
Tolerant of contaminants — open passages pass small wear particles without the scoring/jamming that fine PD clearances suffer.
Simple, safe control — output set by throttling without over-pressure danger.
Direct high-speed drive — couples straight to a motor, avoiding the reduction gearing a PD pump often needs.

**Trade-off:** not self-priming and delivery falls if head rises — not significant for a flooded-suction, low-head circulating duty, so the centrifugal is preferred.
examiner_focus: Multi-staging is a recurring trap: many candidates think it increases flow rather than head/pressure, and some think it means two separate pumps in series rather than impellers mounted in series on one shaft, each feeding the next.

canonical_answers.title: Principle & Relief Valve; Impeller Types; Cavitation
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Principle and relief valve**
The impeller imparts velocity to the liquid, converted to pressure in the volute/diffuser. No relief valve is needed because the pump can only develop its fixed shut-off head; if the discharge is closed it merely churns the liquid and cannot over-pressurise itself as a PD pump would.

**(b) Two impeller types and applications**
Open (or semi-open) impeller — little/no shrouding; unobstructed passages pass solids and fibres without clogging, so best for dirty or solids-laden liquids (bilge, sludge, sewage). Lower efficiency and more clearance-sensitive.
Closed (shrouded) impeller — vanes enclosed between shrouds give defined passages and minimal internal leakage; highest efficiency on clean liquids (sea-water and fresh-water cooling, L.O. service).

Other valid answers: double-entry (high capacity, e.g. main SW circulating) and multi-stage (high head, e.g. boiler feed).

**(c) Cavitation — why it occurs and how it is reduced**
**Why:** as liquid accelerates into the eye its pressure falls; if it reaches the liquid's vapour pressure the liquid flashes into vapour bubbles. Carried into the higher-pressure impeller, these bubbles collapse (implode), causing rattling noise, vibration, loss of head/flow and pitting/erosion of impeller and casing. It occurs whenever NPSHa falls below NPSHr.

**Reduced by design:**
Lower the pump's NPSHr — larger impeller eye, lower speed, or a double-entry impeller (halves inlet velocity); an inducer on critical duties.
Improve the suction installation to raise NPSHa — flooded suction, pressurised suction vessel, short large-bore low-loss piping.
Limit the liquid temperature where possible (lower vapour pressure = greater margin).
examiner_focus: Two things reliably cost marks here: (i) candidates give single-entry/double-entry as the 'two impeller types' asked for, when these are both variations of the fully-shrouded type -- the real types are open, semi-shrouded and fully-shrouded; (ii) cavitation gets defined as bubble formation alone, when the question wants the damage caused by the bubbles collapsing.

canonical_answers.title: Pump Selection (Including Cargo Oil Stripping)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Bilge pumping**
Reciprocating pump — self-priming with good suction lift; handles dirty, solids-laden water.
Centrifugal pump (with priming aid) — large-volume dewatering; open/non-clog impeller passes small debris.

**(b) Cargo oil stripping**
Reciprocating pump — strongly self-priming, drawing the last residues from a nearly empty tank against an air/oil mixture.
Screw pump (PD) — maintains suction and steady delivery at the low flows/high suction lift of stripping, and handles viscous oil. (A self-priming centrifugal stripping pump is also used.)

**(c) Sewage sludge**
Progressive cavity (mono) pump — gentle, non-clogging handling of thick solids-laden sludge.
Diaphragm pump — self-priming, tolerates abrasive/stringy solids and dry running. (Vortex-impeller centrifugal acceptable.)

**(d) Lubricating oil circulating**
Screw pump — smooth pulsation-free delivery of viscous oil; steady bearing pressure.
Gear pump — constant delivery against system resistance; handles high viscosity.

**(e) Sea water circulating**
Centrifugal pump — large volumes of low-viscosity water at low/moderate head; reliable continuous duty.
Axial-flow (propeller) pump — very high flow at low head for large SW circulating duties.
examiner_focus: Well-answered variant of the standard pump-selection question; cargo-oil stripping (screw or reciprocating, for its very low NPSH requirement and ability to run near-dry) is the one application candidates sometimes fumble against the more familiar five-application list.

canonical_answers.title: Two Priming Systems and Their Advantages
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Two priming systems**

**1. Central priming system (vacuum / air-pump type).** A single air-extraction system primes several pumps. A common priming main connects to the top of each pump casing, and a continuously available air pump — usually a liquid-ring (water-ring) type — maintains a vacuum in it. When a pump is to be primed, its connection opens (often automatically on start); the air pump draws air from the casing and suction line into the main, so the pressure falls and liquid is drawn up to fill the casing. A float-operated priming valve on each pump closes when water reaches it (preventing carry-over to the air pump) and reopens if air later collects, so the system re-primes automatically. The liquid-ring air pump uses a vaned rotor running eccentrically, the ring of sealing water forming moving "liquid pistons" that draw and expel air.

**2. Self-priming pump (recirculation type).** The casing retains a charge of water when stopped. On starting with air in the suction, the impeller mixes this air with the retained water into an emulsion, discharged into an internal separation chamber. There the velocity falls; air separates and escapes to discharge while the heavier water drops back and is recirculated to the eye to repeat the cycle. Each pass removes more air, progressively lowering suction pressure and drawing the liquid up; once solid liquid arrives, recirculation ceases and it runs as a normal centrifugal. The only requirement is the initial water charge.

**(b) Advantages of each**
**Central priming system:** one air pump serves many pumps — economical, no priming gear duplicated; standard high-efficiency (non-self-priming) centrifugals can be used. Primes quickly and re-primes automatically when air collects — well suited to air-prone duties (e.g. the bilge main) and lets pumps sit above the liquid without foot valves.
**Self-priming pump:** self-contained — no separate vacuum pump, priming main, float valves or foot valve; less to install, maintain and fail. Independent — unaffected by failure of any central system and recovers its own prime after losing suction; convenient for standalone or portable duties.
examiner_focus: Watch for candidates defaulting to a generic NPSH/cavitation answer instead of actually describing the two priming SYSTEMS asked for (e.g. central vacuum-priming vs self-priming/water-ring) and their respective advantages.

canonical_answers.title: Performance Assessment; Aligning a Replacement Motor
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Assessing performance without dismantling**
Developed head and flow — at known speed read suction/discharge pressures and flow; a fall for the same speed (or low shut-off pressure) points to internal wear.
Power/current — a change for a given duty indicates altered condition.
Vibration, noise and bearing temperature — reveal imbalance, worn bearings, misalignment, cavitation and bearing distress.

**(b) Effects of misalignment**
Heavy vibration, noise, higher power consumption; rapid bearing wear and premature failure; mechanical seal damage and leakage, coupling wear/fretting; in severe cases shaft fatigue and fracture.

**(c) Aligning the replacement motor**
The pump is fixed and the new motor moved to suit. Misalignment is parallel (offset) and/or angular, in both vertical and horizontal planes.
*Sketch instructions: draw the pump (fixed) and the new motor (to be moved) joined by a coupling. Show a rim gauge for radial offset (parallel) and a face gauge for angular error, mounted on the coupling. Show shims under the motor feet for vertical/angular correction and jacking screws for horizontal correction.*

**Prepare** — set the motor and coupling half; clean feet/baseplate/faces; bolts loosely fitted; check for soft foot; set the coupling gap; allow for thermal growth if hot-running.
**Check** — clamp dial gauges across the coupling (rim and face) or use laser; rotate both shafts and read at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° (rim = parallel, face = angular).
**Adjust** — shims under the feet for vertical (equal = parallel, unequal = angular); jacking screws for horizontal.
**Re-check** after each move until within tolerance, tighten and re-check; final check hot where thermal growth is significant.
examiner_focus: The alignment-check sketch is the trap: the magnetic base must sit on the motor shaft with the dial pointer riding on the pump shaft, and the motor shaft is rotated by hand to read run-out. Mounting the gauge on the casing with the pointer on a shaft only proves that shaft isn't bent -- it doesn't check alignment between the two machines.

canonical_answers.title: Axial Piston Hydraulic Pump; Axial vs Radial Pressure
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
In hydraulics the "axial flow" pump here is the axial piston pump; its "radial flow counterpart" is the radial piston pump — both positive-displacement.

**(a) Constant-speed, uni-directional axial piston pump**
A fixed-displacement (swash-plate) axial piston pump has a cylinder barrel carrying a ring of pistons arranged axially around and parallel to the drive shaft. The barrel is rotated by the shaft at constant speed; each piston's slipper bears on a stationary, inclined swash plate set at a fixed angle. As the barrel rotates, each piston is drawn out of its bore over half a revolution (suction) and pushed back in over the other half (delivery). A stationary port (valve) plate with two kidney ports connects each cylinder to inlet while filling and to outlet while discharging. With a fixed swash angle and one direction of rotation the pump delivers a constant flow in one direction. An odd number of pistons (e.g. 7 or 9) smooths delivery. It is compact, high-speed and high-pressure — suited to hydraulic power packs (steering gear, deck machinery).
*Sketch instructions: draw a rotating cylinder barrel with an odd number of pistons arranged parallel to a central drive shaft. Show the pistons' slippers bearing against a stationary swash plate set at a fixed angle. Show a stationary port plate with two kidney-shaped ports, one connected to suction (in), one to delivery (HP out). Label: drive shaft, swash plate (fixed angle), pistons, cylinder barrel (rotates), port (valve) plate, suction (in), delivery (HP out).*

**(b) Why the axial type achieves higher pressure**
Both are positive-displacement; what limits them is how the reaction to the piston's pumping force is carried by the running gear.
*Sketch instructions: two side-by-side diagrams. Axial piston: show the pumping force F = P×A acting as a direct end-thrust along the piston axis onto the swash plate, with only a small side load F·tanα. Radial piston: show the pumping force acting radially against a cam/reaction ring, generating a large radial reaction plus a tangential side load from rotation.*

In the axial piston pump the pumping force F = P×A acts along the piston as a direct end-thrust onto the swash plate, taken by a large thrust bearing, so the piston is loaded essentially in pure compression. The only transverse load is F·tanα (swash angle α ≤ ~18°, tanα ≈ 0.3), so the running gear is lightly side-loaded and can take very high pressures (commonly 300–400 bar).

In the radial piston pump the force acts radially against an eccentric cam/reaction ring through a small line contact; because the block rotates relative to that surface, each piston also carries a tangential side load, and the radial reactions combine into a large unbalanced side load on the eccentric/shaft bearing. The resulting bending and high contact stresses set a lower safe-pressure limit. Hence, for comparable size, the axial arrangement transmits the load as a well-supported axial thrust with minimal side loading, allowing higher working pressure.
examiner_focus: An often-avoided question -- many candidates sketch a hydraulic circuit rather than the pump itself. The mark-earning detail is that the swash (tilting) plate stays stationary while the cylinder block rotates, so the control lever attaches to the swash plate, not to anything on the rotating block.

canonical_answers.title: Affinity Laws; Impeller Trimming; Two-Speed vs Throttling
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Affinity laws**
For a fixed impeller, relating performance to speed N:
Flow proportional to speed: Q ∝ N
Head proportional to speed squared: H ∝ N²
Power proportional to speed cubed: P ∝ N³
So doubling the speed doubles flow, quadruples head, and increases power eight-fold.

**(b) Fitting a slightly smaller diameter impeller**
The same relationships apply to impeller diameter D at constant speed: Q ∝ D · H ∝ D² · P ∝ D³
A slightly smaller (trimmed) impeller gives a modest reduction in flow, a larger reduction in head, and the greatest reduction in power — a permanent way to reduce capacity and head to suit a system without changing speed.

**(c) Two-speed operation versus throttling**
Duty is set where the pump curve meets the system resistance curve (friction head rising with flow squared). Lower flow comes either from throttling a valve or reducing speed.

*Head/Flow diagram: at full speed the duty is at point A. Throttling steepens the system curve and slides the duty up curve N1 to point B — low flow but high head, with the surplus head (B to C) wasted across the valve while the pump still absorbs near full power. Reducing speed drops the pump curve to N2, meeting the original system curve at point C — same low flow, much lower head.*

With P ∝ N³, halving speed cuts power to about an eighth. For a large SW circulating pump swinging between high and low capacity, the cube-law saving makes two-speed clearly preferable to continuous throttle losses; the only limitation is two fixed operating points, adequate for a two-level cooling duty.
examiner_focus: Parts (a)-(b) (affinity laws, effect of impeller trimming) are reliable marks; part (c) is where marks are lost -- candidates often fail to state clearly that throttling wastes power across the valve while the pump still absorbs near-full power, which is the actual reason two-speed operation is preferable for swinging high/low capacity duties.

canonical_answers.title: Laboratory Tests on Ship's Plate Steel + Brittle Fracture Features
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Laboratory tests on steel for ships' plate**
**Tensile test.** A standard test piece is pulled to failure to determine the yield stress, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), percentage elongation and reduction in area. This verifies the steel meets the specified strength requirements and gives a measure of its ductility.
**Bend test.** A specimen is bent cold (typically through 180° around a former). It checks ductility and soundness — the outer fibres must stretch without cracking, confirming freedom from surface defects, laminations or excessive brittleness.
**Notched-bar impact test (Charpy V-notch).** A notched specimen is struck and the energy absorbed in fracture is measured, usually over a range of temperatures. This establishes the toughness/notch ductility and the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature — critical for ship plate, which must resist brittle fracture in cold sea conditions.
**Hardness test (Brinell/Vickers).** Gives a quick indication of strength and, importantly, the uniformity of the material across the plate. Useful for checking heat-affected zones and weldability.
**Chemical analysis.** Confirms the composition (carbon, manganese, sulphur, phosphorus, etc.) lies within specified limits, since composition governs strength, weldability and resistance to brittle fracture.
**Metallographic examination & NDT.** Micro-examination reveals grain size, inclusions and segregation; ultrasonic testing detects internal flaws and laminations that would weaken the plate.

Any six of the above, with reasons, will cover the marks.

**(b) Four features confirming brittle fracture**
Absence of plastic deformation — little or no necking, thinning or reduction in cross-sectional area; the broken pieces fit back together almost exactly.
Bright, granular/crystalline appearance of the fracture face, rather than the dull, fibrous, torn appearance of a ductile failure.
Chevron (herringbone/arrowhead) markings on the surface, which point back towards the origin of the crack.
Fracture plane normal to the applied tensile stress — a flat, square-edged break with no shear lips, and evidence of rapid crack propagation (often initiated at a notch, defect or at low temperature).
examiner_focus: Despite recurring in past diets, this scores poorly -- candidates list the lab tests (tensile, impact, hardness, etc.) but fail to state WHY each test is done, and can't reliably describe the fracture-surface features (bright/crystalline, chevron marks, little/no necking) that indicate brittle failure.

canonical_answers.title: Stress/Strain Curve for Mild Steel
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: plot stress (vertical) against strain (horizontal). Show the straight elastic line from the origin O to a proportional limit A, then elastic limit B, an upper yield point C (where load drops suddenly) and lower yield point D, rising to the ultimate (maximum) stress at E, then falling as necking occurs to fracture at F. Label O, A, B, C, D, E, F.*

**(b)(i) Modulus of Elasticity**
The slope of the straight-line portion O–A, where stress is directly proportional to strain (Hooke's Law). E = stress / strain (in the elastic region). A measure of the stiffness of the material — its resistance to elastic (recoverable) deformation. For mild steel E ≈ 200–210 GN/m². The steeper the line O–A, the stiffer the material.

**(b)(ii) Percentage Elongation**
A measure of ductility — how much the specimen stretches permanently before fracture (point F). % Elongation = (final gauge length − original gauge length) / original gauge length × 100. The two broken halves are fitted back together and the final gauge length measured. For mild steel this is typically around 20–25%. A high value indicates a tough, ductile material that gives ample warning before failing.

**(b)(iii) Ultimate Tensile Stress (UTS)**
Corresponds to the highest point on the curve, E — the maximum load the specimen carries divided by its original cross-sectional area. Beyond E, localised "necking" begins; the reduced area means the load falls off (E→F) even though the true stress in the neck is still rising, and the specimen finally fractures at F. UTS is the figure quoted for the strength of the steel.

**(b)(iv) Yield Stress**
The stress at which the material begins to deform plastically — permanent strain sets in. On the mild-steel curve this is the distinct yield region: an upper yield point C where the load drops suddenly, followed by a lower yield point D at which strain increases with little or no increase in stress. Below the yield stress the steel returns to its original length when unloaded; above it the deformation is permanent. It is the key design figure, as structures are kept safely below yield.
examiner_focus: Sketch-dependent question: candidates who don't annotate the stress/strain curve lose the ability to reference it in part (b) and effectively answer blind. A recurring wrong sketch is the creep (strain-time) curve instead of the stress/strain curve.

canonical_answers.title: Shipboard Applications of Metals
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Stainless Steel** — Application: galley equipment, food/freshwater storage tanks and pipework; also fresh/sea water pump shafts and valve spindles. Reason: high chromium content (≥12%) forms a self-healing passive oxide film giving excellent corrosion resistance to water, salt and foodstuffs; keeps surfaces hygienic and maintains good strength with an easily-washed finish.

**(b) Grey Cast Iron** — Application: engine cylinder liners, cylinder blocks, bedplates and pump/valve bodies. Reason: free graphite flakes give self-lubricating properties, excellent wear resistance and high damping capacity to absorb vibration; good compressive strength, cheap and easily cast into complex shapes — though brittle and weak in tension.

**(c) Titanium** — Application: plate-type heat exchangers and seawater cooler plates. Reason: outstanding seawater corrosion resistance combined with a very high strength-to-weight ratio, allowing thin plates with excellent heat transfer that resist erosion/corrosion with little maintenance, despite high initial cost.

**(d) Manganese Bronze** — Application: ship's propellers (especially smaller ones). Reason: a high-tensile brass offering good strength, toughness and ductility with excellent corrosion and cavitation-erosion resistance in seawater; casts well into large complex shapes and resists the fatigue stresses of the propeller's working environment.

**(e) Aluminium** — Application: superstructure, deckhouses, lifeboats and ladders. Reason: low density (about one-third that of steel) reduces topside weight, lowering the centre of gravity and improving stability, and cutting fuel consumption; forms a protective oxide film giving good marine-atmosphere corrosion resistance, with alloying restoring adequate strength.
examiner_focus: Two specific traps recur: stainless steel gets wrongly restricted to small-vessel propellers when the question asks about LARGE propellers (its actual edge is harsh/icy environments), and nickel-aluminium-bronze's key selling point -- that it's easily repairable -- is rarely mentioned.

canonical_answers.title: Creep and Fatigue (with graph)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Creep**
Definition: creep is the slow, continuous plastic (permanent) deformation of a material under a constant load (stress) over a long period at elevated temperature, occurring even when the applied stress is well below the yield stress. For steels it becomes significant above roughly 0.4 × the melting temperature (absolute), typically above ~350–400°C.

*Graph: plot strain (vertical) against time (horizontal). Show an initial instantaneous strain step at t=0, then a Primary stage where the rate is high but falling, a Secondary stage that is the long straight portion at constant minimum rate, and a Tertiary stage that curves sharply upward to rupture.*

Primary (transient) creep: strain rate is initially high but decreases as the material work-hardens. Secondary (steady-state) creep: the rate is constant and minimum — work-hardening balanced by recovery; the longest stage, and its slope is the design figure used to predict service life. Tertiary creep: the rate accelerates rapidly as necking, voids and cracking develop, leading to rupture. The higher the temperature and/or stress, the steeper the curve and the sooner failure occurs.

**Practical example:** exhaust valves, exhaust valve spindles and superheater/boiler tubes — high temperature plus sustained pressure causes gradual stretching. Burnt boiler tubes that "bag" or balloon outwards are a classic creep failure.

**(b) Fatigue**
Definition: fatigue is failure under repeated, fluctuating or reversed (cyclic) loading at a stress below the ultimate tensile — often below the yield — stress. A tiny crack initiates at a stress concentration, propagates a little with each cycle, and the component finally fractures suddenly when the remaining cross-section can no longer carry the load.

*Graph: the S–N (Wöhler) curve — stress amplitude (vertical) vs number of cycles to failure on a log scale (horizontal). The curve falls as stress reduces, then flattens to a horizontal fatigue (endurance) limit, below which the material has effectively infinite life.*

Fracture face: a smooth area showing "beach marks"/conchoidal lines radiating from the origin, plus a rough crystalline area of final rapid fracture. Cracks start at keyways, sharp corners, threads, weld defects, corrosion pits or tool marks.

**Practical example:** crankshafts (at fillet radii between journals and webs), propeller-shaft failures, or fluctuating-load bolts. Generous fillet radii and polished surfaces are the main preventives.

**Key difference:** creep is time and temperature dependent (static load); fatigue is cycle dependent (dynamic/repeated load).
examiner_focus: Creep (a) loses marks for omitting temperature as a factor and for sketching a stress/strain curve instead of a creep curve; fatigue (b) loses marks for omitting a practical example even when the beach-mark fracture sketch is correct. A graph is genuinely expected for both parts even when not explicitly requested.

canonical_answers.title: Creep — Strain-Time Curve (Supplied)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
The curve plots strain against time under a constant load at elevated temperature, and reads through four features: Initial strain (elastic + plastic) — the instantaneous strain produced the moment the load is applied, before any time-dependent creep begins. Primary (transient) creep — strain rate starts high but progressively decreases as the material work-hardens. Secondary (steady-state) creep — the long, straight portion of constant minimum slope, work-hardening balanced by thermal recovery; the most important region, since its slope (the steady creep rate) is used to predict service life. Tertiary creep — the rate accelerates rapidly as voids, necking and internal cracking develop, terminating at rupture.

**Key point:** creep is permanent plastic deformation occurring under a steady stress below the yield point, given enough time at temperature.
**Practical example:** superheater/boiler tubes and exhaust valves — sustained high temperature plus steady pressure causes gradual stretching (e.g. boiler tubes that "bag" outward over time).
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; treat as a standard creep question -- describe primary/secondary/tertiary stages against the strain-time curve and state that temperature is a key factor, since that link is the one candidates most often omit elsewhere in this topic.

canonical_answers.title: S–N (Wöhler) Fatigue Curve
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Definition: fatigue is failure of a component under repeated, fluctuating or reversed (cyclic) loading, at a stress below the ultimate tensile — often below the yield — stress. A microscopic crack initiates at a stress concentration, propagates with each cycle, and the component fails by sudden fracture once the remaining cross-section can no longer carry the load.

Reading the graph: stress amplitude (S) is plotted against number of cycles to failure (N), with N on a logarithmic scale. As applied stress is reduced, cycles survived increase, so the curve falls steeply through the finite-life region. For ferrous metals the curve then becomes horizontal: this level is the fatigue (endurance) limit. Below it the steel endures an effectively infinite number of cycles. Designing below this limit prevents fatigue failure.

Fatigue fracture appearance: a smooth area with "beach marks"/conchoidal lines radiating from the crack origin (slow growth), plus a rough crystalline area where final rapid fracture occurred. Cracks start at stress raisers — keyways, sharp corners, threads, weld defects, corrosion pits or tool marks.

**Practical example:** crankshafts (failing at the fillet radii between journals and webs), propeller-shaft failures, or fluctuating-load bolts. Main preventives: reduce stress concentrations via generous fillet radii, polished surfaces and good surface finish.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the fatigue/endurance limit is the mark-earning feature of the S-N curve -- for steels the curve flattens to a stress below which failure won't occur regardless of cycle count, unlike non-ferrous metals which have no true limit.

canonical_answers.title: Fatigue — LCF/HCF and Finite/Infinite Life
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Definition: fatigue is failure of a component under repeated, fluctuating or reversed (cyclic) loading, at a stress below the ultimate tensile — often below the yield — stress. A tiny crack initiates at a stress concentration, grows a little with each cycle, and the part fails by sudden fracture when the remaining section can no longer carry the load.

**High-stress/low-N end:** at high stress the material survives only a few cycles; the curve sits high and flat at top left. The region left of ~10³–10⁴ cycles is Low Cycle Fatigue (LCF) — large stresses (often into the plastic range), few cycles. Typical of occasional heavy overloads or thermal cycling.

**Falling portion:** as stress is reduced, cycles survived rise sharply; the curve sweeps downward. The region beyond ~10⁴–10⁵ cycles is High Cycle Fatigue (HCF) — lower stresses, very large numbers of cycles, essentially elastic. Covers most rotating/vibrating machinery.

**The horizontal fatigue (endurance) limit:** the curve flattens at ~10⁶–10^7 cycles and becomes horizontal. Above it is the finite-life zone (eventual failure after a calculable number of cycles); below it is the infinite-life zone — the steel endures effectively unlimited cycles.

Fracture appearance: a smooth area with "beach marks" radiating from the origin, plus a rough crystalline area of final rupture.

**Practical example:** crankshafts failing at journal/web fillet radii (also propeller-shaft and connecting-rod bolt failures). Preventives: generous fillet radii, good surface finish, removal of stress concentrations.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the LCF/HCF split and finite-vs-infinite-life regions are the mark-earning distinction -- low-cycle fatigue involves higher stress/plastic strain and short life, high-cycle fatigue involves lower stress, elastic strain, and (for ferrous materials) a stress level below which life becomes effectively infinite.

canonical_answers.title: Air Receivers — Corrosion, Prevention, Safe Interim Use
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why air receivers are prone to corrosion**
The air delivered by the compressor contains moisture (water vapour). As the air is compressed and cools in the receiver, this moisture condenses out as water, collecting at the bottom. Liquid water in contact with the steel — together with oxygen in the compressed air — provides the classic conditions for electrochemical (wet) corrosion. In addition, the air carries traces of oil carried over from the compressor, and the moisture may be slightly acidic, accelerating attack. Corrosion concentrates at the bottom of the receiver and around the drain, worsened if the receiver is not drained regularly.

**(b) How corrosion can be prevented**
Drain the receiver regularly of accumulated water and oil — the single most important measure (automatic drain traps, routine manual draining, slight slope toward the drain).
Remove moisture before the air enters by fitting effective inter-/after-coolers with moisture separators (and air dryers where fitted) on the compressor delivery.
Protect the internal surfaces with a corrosion-resistant coating/paint or galvanising, inspected and maintained at survey.

**(c) Safe use in service until a permanent repair**
Establish the remaining metal thickness by ultrasonic thickness testing over the affected area, and calculate the wall thickness still required to contain the working pressure safely with an adequate margin.
Reduce the maximum working pressure — allow the receiver to remain in service at a reduced (de-rated) working pressure, with the safety valve re-set to the new lower pressure.
Re-set/verify safety devices and increase monitoring — confirm the safety valve lifts at the de-rated pressure, drain frequently, inspect the corroded area more often.
Obtain Classification Society/Surveyor agreement — continued use at reduced pressure must be documented and approved, clearly marked on the vessel, with a permanent repair carried out at the earliest opportunity.

**Principle:** since bursting pressure depends on wall thickness, reducing the working pressure in proportion to the lost thickness restores an acceptable safety margin until the vessel can be properly repaired.
examiner_focus: Generally solid answers, with sketches of the corrosion-prevention/interim-repair arrangements being the weaker element.

canonical_answers.title: Metallurgical Processes — Induction Hardening, Nitriding, Case Hardening
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Induction Hardening**
A surface-hardening process applied to medium/high-carbon steels. The component is surrounded by a water-cooled copper coil (inductor) carrying a high-frequency alternating current, inducing eddy currents that rapidly heat a thin surface layer above its upper critical temperature while the core stays cool. The surface is then immediately quenched. Result: a hard, wear-resistant martensitic surface layer over a tough, ductile core. Depth is controlled by current frequency and heating time. Rapid, localised, and well suited to gear teeth, crankshaft journals and cam surfaces.

**(b) Nitriding**
A surface-hardening process that introduces nitrogen, carried out on special alloy steels containing nitride-forming elements (aluminium, chromium, molybdenum — "Nitralloy" steels). The finished, heat-treated component is held at a relatively low temperature (~500°C) in an ammonia atmosphere for a prolonged period; the ammonia dissociates and nitrogen diffuses into the surface, forming extremely hard, wear-resistant nitrides. Advantages: low temperature and no quenching, so minimal distortion; the surface retains hardness at elevated temperature with good corrosion and fatigue resistance. Used for valve spindles, gears and crankshafts. Main drawback: the process is slow.

**(c) Case Hardening**
Produces a hard, high-carbon surface "case" on a tough, low-carbon steel core. Two stages: **1. Carburising** — heated to ~900–950°C in a carbon-rich medium (solid, liquid or gaseous) so carbon diffuses into the surface layer; longer time and higher temperature give a deeper case. **2. Hardening** — the carbon-enriched surface is heated above its critical temperature and quenched, transforming the high-carbon case into hard martensite while the low-carbon core stays soft and tough, often followed by a refining/tempering treatment. Result: a hard, wear-resistant outer case with a tough, ductile core — typical applications being gudgeon pins, gears, cams and bearing surfaces.
examiner_focus: A rarely-attempted question -- most candidates skip it rather than answer poorly, suggesting the three named heat-treatment processes (induction hardening, nitriding, case hardening) aren't well revised as a set.

canonical_answers.title: Class 1 Pressure Vessel — Test Pieces and Tests
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) How the test pieces are obtained**
For a Class 1 (fusion-welded) pressure vessel, weld quality must be proved by destructive testing. Since specimens cannot be cut from the finished vessel, a separate test plate is welded on as a continuation of an actual production seam.
*Sketch instructions: draw a test plate (~300mm wide) butted up to and welded as an extension of a vessel's main longitudinal seam. Mark out and number the specimen locations across the weld: (1) a dog-bone profiled transverse tensile specimen; (2) two plain rectangular strips for bend tests (root bend, face bend); (3) a further reduced-section tensile/all-weld-metal specimen; (4) and (5) small notched strips for impact (Charpy) tests from the weld metal and HAZ. Mark a lower spare portion reserved for retests.*

**Preparing the test plate.** A test plate is butted up to and welded integrally with the end of one of the vessel's main (longitudinal) seams, forming a natural run-off extension. This guarantees identical conditions — same parent plate, edge preparation, welding procedure, consumables, welder, pre-heat and heat treatment.
**Heat treatment and NDT.** The test plate undergoes any stress-relieving/heat treatment given to the vessel, and is then radiographed (and/or ultrasonically examined) along with the seam to confirm soundness before specimens are cut.
**Retest material.** A lower portion is reserved spare material "for retests if necessary," so duplicate pieces can be cut from the same proven plate should any specimen fail or give a doubtful result.

**(b) Tests carried out**
Transverse tensile test — across the weld, to verify the joint meets specified UTS (ideally failing in the parent metal, not the weld).
Bend tests — a root bend and a face bend (and/or a side bend on thick plate), proving ductility and soundness.
Impact (Charpy V-notch) test — notched pieces broken to measure toughness/notch ductility of the weld metal and HAZ.
Macro-examination (and hardness) test — a section polished, etched and examined for penetration, fusion, freedom from cracks/porosity/slag and correct profile, often with a hardness survey across weld, parent metal and HAZ.
examiner_focus: The whole question hinges on part (a): candidates who correctly sketch and identify where the test pieces are cut from the parent plate can carry that straight into full marks on part (b) (which just asks for the tests run on those pieces), while candidates who skip or botch part (a) -- including sketches showing the test pieces cut from off the plate -- collapse to one-word guesses in part (b).

canonical_answers.title: Types of Stress and Strain; Tests on Ship's Side Plating
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Three Types of Stress**
Stress is the internal resistance per unit area set up against an applied load: stress = load ÷ cross-sectional area (N/m²).
Tensile stress — set up by a pulling (stretching) load along the axis, tending to lengthen the material. Example: a tie-bar, or the lower fibres of a sagging hull.
Compressive stress — set up by a pushing (squeezing) load, tending to shorten or crush. Example: a pillar/stanchion, or deck plating of a sagging hull.
Shear stress — set up when equal, opposite and parallel loads act across a section, tending to make one part slide over the adjacent part. Example: the cross-section of a rivet or bolt.

Bending and torsional/twisting stress are equally acceptable as a third type.

**(a)(ii) Two Types of Strain**
Strain is the deformation produced by the stress, expressed as a ratio (no units).
Direct (linear) strain — change in length per unit original length produced by tensile or compressive stress: strain = change in length / original length. Tensile strain is an extension; compressive strain a shortening.
Shear strain — the angular distortion produced by a shear stress, measured as the angle (radians) through which a face is displaced relative to the original right angle.

Volumetric strain (change in volume ÷ original volume) is an acceptable alternative.

**(b) Tests on steel for ship's side plating**
Tensile test — a machined test piece pulled to destruction to find yield stress, UTS, percentage elongation and reduction in area.
Bend test — a strip bent cold around a former to confirm ductility and soundness.
Impact (Charpy V-notch) test — notched specimens broken over a range of temperatures to establish the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
Chemical analysis — confirms composition within specified limits, governing strength, weldability and brittle-fracture resistance.
Hardness test and NDT/examination — hardness checks strength and uniformity; ultrasonic testing detects internal laminations/flaws.
examiner_focus: Part (b) is the weak spot: very few candidates can actually define strain (deformation per unit original length/dimension) despite being comfortable with stress.

canonical_answers.title: Cupro-Nickel, White Metal, Titanium + NAB/Stainless for Large Propellers (apart from corrosion/erosion)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Cupro-Nickel** — a copper-base alloy with nickel (typically 70/30 or 90/10), often with small iron and manganese additions. Outstanding resistance to seawater corrosion and erosion, particularly impingement attack by fast-flowing water, with good ductility and reasonable strength; resists biofouling. Example: seawater pipework and condenser/cooler tubes and tube plates.

**(a)(ii) White Metal** — a soft tin- or lead-based bearing alloy (Babbitt), with antimony and copper. Low coefficient of friction, good embeddability and conformability; bonds readily to a stronger backing shell. Example: lining of main and bottom-end (white-metalled) and crosshead bearings.

**(a)(iii) Titanium** — outstanding strength-to-weight ratio and exceptional seawater corrosion resistance from a stable, self-healing oxide film. Retains strength at temperature but costly and difficult to machine. Example: plate-type heat exchangers/seawater cooler plates.

**(b)(i) Nickel-aluminium Bronze** (apart from corrosion/erosion) — high strength-to-weight ratio with excellent toughness and ductility, so it withstands fluctuating (fatigue) loads and occasional impact without cracking. Good fatigue strength and cavitation resistance, and casts well into the large, complex curved blade shapes required.

**(b)(ii) Stainless Steel** (apart from corrosion) — propeller-grade (often cast martensitic/duplex) stainless steel provides high tensile strength and hardness, allowing thinner, more efficient blade sections for the same strength. Good toughness and fatigue resistance for cyclic loading, excellent cavitation-erosion resistance, and a hard surface that polishes smooth and is readily repaired by welding.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the trap shared with the near-identical Q17 is that stainless steel and NAB are asked about beyond corrosion/erosion resistance -- for large propellers, focus on strength, repairability (NAB) and suitability for harsh/icy conditions (stainless) rather than repeating the corrosion-resistance answer already excluded by the question.

canonical_answers.title: Brittle vs Ductile Failure; Ductile-Brittle Transition; Charpy Test
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Brittle Failure**
A sudden, rapid fracture with little or no plastic deformation beforehand. The crack propagates very quickly, often at stresses below the yield point, giving no warning. The fracture face is bright, granular/crystalline, the break roughly square to the applied stress, and the pieces fit back together almost exactly (no necking). Promoted by low temperature, notches/stress raisers and shock loading.

**(a)(ii) Ductile Failure**
Occurs only after considerable plastic deformation. The material stretches, yields and necks down before tearing, absorbing a large amount of energy and giving plenty of visible warning. The fracture face is dull, fibrous and rough, often with a characteristic "cup-and-cone" shape and shear lips. The desirable, "safe" mode of failure.

**(b) Ductile-to-Brittle Transition**
Many steels are ductile and tough at higher temperatures but become brittle as temperature falls. The transition is the change in behaviour over a narrow temperature band: above it failure is tough and ductile (high energy); below it the same steel fails in a brittle manner (low energy). The determining factor is temperature — specifically the transition temperature. For ship steels this must be kept safely below the lowest expected service (seawater) temperature; composition (lower carbon, added Mn/Ni) and fine grain size are used to lower it.

**(c) Charpy Impact Test**
Specimen: a standard bar (10mm×10mm×55mm) with a V-notch machined at its centre to act as a controlled stress raiser. Apparatus: supported horizontally as a simple beam in the anvil of a pendulum impact-testing machine, notch on the face opposite the side to be struck. The test: a heavy pendulum/striker, released from a known height, swings down and breaks the specimen in one blow; the energy absorbed (joules) is read from the machine scale. Interpretation: a high energy value indicates tough/ductile behaviour, a low value brittle. Repeating over a range of temperatures and plotting energy vs temperature gives the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
examiner_focus: A popular, generally well-answered question, but three specific slips recur: brittle/ductile failure descriptions stay too shallow, the temperature link in the ductile-to-brittle transition gets omitted, and the named test in part (c) should be the Charpy V-notch test specifically, not just 'an impact test.'

canonical_answers.title: Properties of Materials — Strength, Hardness, Ductility, Toughness, Brittleness
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Strength** — the ability to withstand an applied load without failing. Measured as the stress the material can carry, quoted as tensile, compressive or shear strength. Ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress sustained before failure.

**(b) Hardness** — the ability to resist surface indentation, scratching, abrasion and wear. Measured by pressing a standard indenter into the surface (Brinell, Vickers or Rockwell). Hardness generally rises with strength but usually with reduced ductility. Important for wearing surfaces such as gear teeth and journals.

**(c) Ductility** — the ability to undergo considerable plastic deformation before fracture. Measured by percentage elongation and percentage reduction in area in a tensile test. Mild steel and copper are good examples.

**(d) Toughness** — the ability to absorb energy, particularly from shock or impact, without fracturing, by deforming plastically. Combines reasonable strength with good ductility and resists crack propagation. Measured by the energy absorbed in an impact (Charpy/Izod) test. Essential for shock-loaded parts such as crankshafts and gears.

**(e) Brittleness** — the tendency to fracture suddenly with little or no plastic deformation. A brittle material gives no warning, fails at low energy, and the broken faces fit back together almost exactly. Examples: grey cast iron, glass, hardened steel.
examiner_focus: This is the textbook example of 'describe' vs 'state': giving the bare definition (e.g. 'strength is the ability to resist force without rupture') earns half marks, and the second mark only comes from adding the extra qualifying detail (e.g. naming that the force may be tensile, compressive or shear).
