canonical_answers.title: Static OWS — Operation with Pump on Discharge Side
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Same underlying content as Q1 above, with the emphasis specifically on the pump being on the discharge (downstream) side of the vessel.

Because the pump is on the discharge side, the unit operates under suction — water is drawn through rather than pushed in. A pump placed before the separator would shear and agitate the oil into a fine, stable emulsion the coalescer struggles to break; drawing water through under low-velocity suction keeps oil droplets intact and easy to separate. The rest of the operation (gravity chamber, separating matrix, polishing pack, oil sensing probe and outlet valve, OCM and 3-way valve) follows as in Q1.
examiner_focus: The question specifies the pump on the DISCHARGE side of the separator -- candidates who sketch other pump arrangements (e.g. pump on the suction/inlet side) lose marks even if the rest of the sketch is otherwise correct.

canonical_answers.title: Static Oily Water Separators — Pump Selection, Separation Mechanism, Fluid Properties
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why the supply pump must be carefully selected.** A pump that shears or agitates the mixture (e.g. a centrifugal pump pushing oily water into the separator) will emulsify the oil into a fine, stable dispersion that the coalescer cannot break. A gentle, low-shear pump (or the pump located on the discharge/suction side) preserves droplet size so gravity and coalescence can work.

**(b) How the separator achieves effective separation.** Gravity settling gives residence time for bulk free oil to rise (Stokes' Law). The coalescing separating matrix merges finer dispersed droplets on its oleophilic surface until buoyant enough to rise. The polishing pack is a finer second coalescing stage bringing the effluent below 15 ppm.

**(c) How physical properties affect rate and effectiveness**
Density difference — the driving force; the greater the difference, the faster oil rises. Heating lowers oil density, increasing the difference.
Viscosity — rise velocity is inversely proportional to viscosity; a viscous oil resists movement and coalescence. Heating cuts viscosity dramatically, aiding separation.
Surface/interfacial tension — governs how readily droplets coalesce; detergents/surfactants lower interfacial tension, stabilising a fine emulsion that resists separation.
Buoyancy — the net upward force on a droplet; because volume rises with the cube of diameter while drag rises only with diameter, larger droplets rise much faster — the reason coalescence (growing droplets) makes separation work.
examiner_focus: Parts (a) and (b) are handled well, but part (c) exposes a real gap -- candidates default to discussing the DENSITY difference between oil and water and rarely mention VISCOSITY, despite viscosity (of both the oil and any emulsion) being just as significant to separation rate and effectiveness.

canonical_answers.title: Hydraulic Oil Reservoir Functions; High Oil Temperature Tripping
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Functions of the hydraulic oil reservoir**
Stores the system's working volume plus reserve, so the level still covers the suction when actuators are fully extended and the pump never draws air.
Allows for thermal expansion and contraction without overflowing or uncovering the suction.
De-aeration — large surface area and dwell time (commonly 3–5 times pump delivery per minute) let entrained air escape before recirculation.
Settling of contaminants and water — dwell time lets solids/water settle to a sloped sump for draining; baffles separate return from suction.
Cooling/heat dissipation — the oil volume and reservoir surface act as a thermal reservoir.
Maintains pump suction head and provides make-up for minor leakage.

**(b) Four reasons for tripping on high oil temperature**
Cooler fault/loss of cooling — fouled cooler, low cooling-water flow, failed cooling-water pump.
Low oil level/insufficient volume — shorter circulation time reduces de-aeration and cooling.
Internal leakage/worn components — worn pump, valves or seals leak high-pressure oil internally, converting pressure energy to heat.
Relief valve passing or set too low, or system overload — oil continuously dumping across the relief valve generates heat.
examiner_focus: This question was previously worth 10 marks for part (a) alone and was judged to demand too much detail, so it's now split 6/4 with an easier part (b) -- results are mixed, roughly split between candidates who adapt well to the reservoir-function angle and those who don't.

canonical_answers.title: Deck Machinery Hydraulic System (Sketch) + Electric vs Hydraulic Advantages
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw a sump/reservoir with suction strainer feeding a variable-delivery, pressure-compensated pump (swash-plate symbol with compensator), through a check valve to a pressure line with a relief valve back to sump, a pressure-line filter, an accumulator on the pressure line, a 3-way hand-operated spring-return directional control valve feeding a double-acting load (motor/ram), with a branch "to other load," and a return line through a return filter back to the sump.*

The pump's pressure compensator senses delivery pressure and reduces the swash angle to near-zero stroke when the set pressure is reached, so it delivers only the flow the system demands; the accumulator then maintains pressure for standby.

**(b) Advantages of electric over hydraulic deck machinery**
No risk of oil pollution — no high-pressure hydraulic oil at deck level, no leak/spill risk overboard.
Higher efficiency, lower running cost — avoids the compounded losses of a hydraulic system and standby power-pack losses.
Less maintenance and no oil system — no power pack, high-pressure piping, hoses or hydraulic filters to maintain.
Better, more precise control — AC variable-frequency drives give fine speed control, regenerative braking and built-in condition-monitoring data.
Cleaner, simpler installation — no long high-pressure piping runs, no cold-weather oil viscosity problems.

Balancing note: hydraulics remain common for their inherent overload protection (relief valve), high power-to-weight ratio, and explosion-safety with no arcing.
examiner_focus: Well answered overall; interestingly, some candidates skip the sketch in part (a) entirely and still pick up full marks on part (b) (advantages of electric over hydraulic deck machinery), since the two parts are marked fairly independently.

canonical_answers.title: Deck Machinery Hydraulic System (Sketch) + Operation of the System
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** As per Q9's sketch above.

**(b) Operation.** The variable-delivery pump draws oil from the sump through the suction strainer and delivers it through the check valve into the pressure line. The compensator senses delivery pressure and adjusts the swash-plate angle to match output to demand; when demand stops and pressure reaches the set value, the compensator destrokes the pump to near-zero flow, so the pump only makes up leakage rather than continuously dumping full flow over the relief valve.

The check valve prevents stored pressure leaking back through the destroked pump. The accumulator holds the system charged while destroked, supplies peak/transient flow demands faster than the pump can stroke up, and absorbs pressure shocks. Operating the directional control valve directs oil to the load; releasing it lets the spring return the valve to neutral (fail-safe). The relief valve protects against overpressure (e.g. a stalled actuator); spent oil returns through the return filter to the sump for de-aeration, settling and cooling.
examiner_focus: No recurring trap noted -- consistently solid answers for both the sketch and the operational description.

canonical_answers.title: Hydraulic Oil Contamination — Types, Effects, Monitoring
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Four types of contamination and how they occur**
Water — condensation in the reservoir, worn seals/glands, leaking coolers, or seawater/rainwater ingress through damaged rod seals.
Solid particles/dirt — grit or weld scale left during manufacture/repair, a defective air breather, or ingress past worn ram-rod wiper seals.
Wear metal — generated internally by wear of pump components, valve spools, bearings and gears.
Air/aeration — drawn in through a low oil level uncovering the suction, a leaking suction-side joint, or insufficient de-aeration time.

**(b) Four effects of oil contamination**
Increased wear and component damage — abrasive solids and wear metal score pistons, spools and seals.
Corrosion — water and acidic oxidation products corrode internal surfaces.
Sluggish, spongy or erratic control — entrained air/water make the oil compressible.
Valve sticking/blockage and filter clogging — particles jam spool valves and block orifices.

**(c) Monitoring for contamination.** Regular sampling and laboratory analysis (water content, viscosity, TAN, particle/wear-metal spectrographic analysis). Onboard checks — visual/crackle test for water, return/pressure filter ΔP indicator, and magnetic plug inspection for wear metal.
examiner_focus: A rarely-attempted question -- low attempt numbers suggest hydraulic-oil contamination types/effects/monitoring isn't a well-revised area, more than it being poorly answered by those who do try.

canonical_answers.title: Fuel Oil Viscosity — Necessity, Measurement Methods, Control Action
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why correct viscosity is necessary.** Viscosity controls atomisation at the injector. Too high (oil too cold) — poor atomisation, after-burning, carbon/soot deposits, loss of power/efficiency. Too low (oil too hot) — poor spray penetration, loss of the lubricating film in the fuel pump/injector, seizure/scuffing risk. Correct viscosity (~10–15 cSt at the injector) is set by controlling fuel temperature.

**(b) Two on-line viscosity measuring methods**
**1. Capillary/differential-pressure type.** A constant-displacement gear pump forces a fixed flow through a fixed-bore capillary tube; by Poiseuille's law, the pressure drop across the tube is directly proportional to viscosity. A differential-pressure transducer gives a continuous pneumatic or electronic signal.
**2. Oscillating/vibrating-element (torsional) type.** A probe with a vibrating element immersed in the fuel is driven at its resonant frequency; viscous drag damps the oscillation, and the power needed to maintain constant amplitude is proportional to viscosity, converted to a continuous 4–20mA output.

**(c) Control action, with reasons.** The controller acts on the fuel heater steam/electrical supply valve: if viscosity is above set point (too cold/thick), it opens the heater valve to raise temperature; if below set point (too hot/thin), it closes the valve. A proportional + integral (PI) action holds viscosity accurately with no offset as load and fuel grade change — viscosity, not temperature, is controlled directly since different fuel grades reach the target viscosity at different temperatures.
examiner_focus: A popular, generally well-scored question, but part (b) is the trap: it asks candidates to DESCRIBE two viscosity-measurement methods suitable for a control system, and marks are lost for merely STATING method names, or for describing a laboratory viscosity TEST rather than an inline measuring device that could actually feed a pneumatic/electronic controller.

canonical_answers.title: Hydrocarbon Tanks — Flammability Terms and Safe Atmosphere
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Same underlying content as the Fire Safety topic's hydrocarbon tanks question (Q8 there) — reproduced here since this reference guide answers it under OWS/Hydraulics/Fuel Oil as well.

**(a)(i) Explosive limits.** LEL/UEL bound the flammable range of hydrocarbon-vapour-in-air concentration.
**(a)(ii) Vapour pressure.** The pressure exerted by a liquid's vapour at equilibrium in an enclosed space at a given temperature; rises with temperature.
**(a)(iii) Flash point.** The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to momentarily flash when an ignition source is applied.

**(b) Maintaining a safe tank atmosphere.** Keep the atmosphere out of the flammable range by controlling oxygen rather than hydrocarbon content: inert gas reduces oxygen below ~5–8%, so no mixture can support combustion whatever the hydrocarbon percentage. Maintain a slight positive IG pressure; purge with inert gas before ventilating to air (never ventilate a hydrocarbon-rich tank directly with air, which would pass through the flammable range).
examiner_focus: Very poorly answered -- most candidates show little grasp of basic hydrocarbon flammability terms (explosive limits, vapour pressure, flash point) or how a tank atmosphere with varying flammable-gas percentage is kept safe (inerting outside the flammable range, not just ventilating).

canonical_answers.title: Bunker Line Pinhole Leak — Immediate Actions and Permanent Repair
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Immediate actions**
Stop bunkering immediately — signal the barge/shore to stop pumping and shut valves to isolate and depressurise the section.
Contain the spill — plug scuppers, deploy the SOPEP spill kit and save-alls.
Raise the alarm/inform — notify the duty officer and Master, muster the spill response team per SOPEP/SMPEP.
Transfer/relieve the line — drain remaining oil from the section, clean up spilled oil retaining it for disposal.

**(b) Permanent repair, precautions and inspections.** A pinhole indicates wall thinning/corrosion — a clamp or weld over the hole is not a permanent fix. Ship's staff renew the affected section: isolate, drain and gas-free the line; cut out the defective section and fabricate a replacement spool of correct material/bore/thickness; weld by a qualified welder, then **pressure-test the new pipe before fitting**; fit with new gaskets and pressure-test the joint in situ.

**Precautions:** hot work permit and fire precautions, gas-free certificate, correct welding procedure and qualified welder.

**Further inspections:** inspect the rest of the bunker pipework — a pinhole from corrosion strongly suggests the remainder is in similar condition, so carry out ultrasonic wall-thickness measurement along the line, especially at low points and bends, renewing any further thin sections found.
examiner_focus: Part (a) (immediate actions) is handled fine; part (b) (permanent repair) is where answers scatter -- a recurring wrong turn is treating the bunker line as a pressure vessel requiring Class notification, when a straightforward fabricated pipe replacement by ship's staff is within scope. The repaired section should be pressure tested before fitting, and the REST of the bunker pipework inspected too, since it may be in similarly degraded condition.

canonical_answers.title: Fuel with High Pour Point — Test and Measures to Enable Use
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Pour point test.** A sample is placed in a standard test jar with a thermometer, first heated to dissolve any wax, then cooled steadily in stages. At each 3°C interval the jar is tilted horizontally for ~5 seconds to check whether the surface moves. Cooling continues until no movement is observed; the pour point is recorded as 3°C above that no-flow temperature.

**(b) Measures to enable use of the fuel.** Keep the fuel above its pour point at every stage: maintain bunker tank temperature (heating coils) at least ~10°C above the pour point; heat-trace and lag transfer lines so fuel doesn't chill/gel in exposed pipe runs; heat settling and service tanks; heat before the purifier for correct separating temperature; final heating at the booster heater to injection viscosity (~10–15 cSt). Avoid cold pockets/dead legs by keeping fuel circulating and flushing lines through with hot fuel when stopping.
examiner_focus: Part (a) catches some candidates describing a VISCOSITY test instead of the pour-point test the question specifically asks about for a high-pour-point fuel.

canonical_answers.title: Microbacterial Infestation — Systems Affected, Conditions, Detection
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Systems affected.** Fuel oil systems (especially distillate/diesel storage tanks); lubricating oil systems; hydraulic oil systems; fresh water/cooling water systems.

**(b) Conditions required for bacteria to evolve.** Water (the essential requirement, especially free water at the oil/water interface); a food source (hydrocarbons plus trace nutrients); a suitable temperature (roughly 20–40°C, exactly the range of bunker/settling/service tanks); oxygen for aerobic types, or oxygen-depleted pockets for anaerobic types (e.g. sulphate-reducing bacteria producing H2S); and stagnant/undisturbed conditions and time for colonies to establish.

**(c) Detecting microbial contamination.** Sampling and laboratory testing — dip-slide/culture kits or laboratory microbiological analysis of a tank-bottom sample. Physical/operational signs — rapid filter blocking, dark slimy sludge at the oil-water interface, increased water content and acidity, unusual smell, evidence of corrosion/pitting.
examiner_focus: Part (a) wants four AFFECTED SYSTEMS specifically (commonly fuel oil, lubricating oil, hydraulic oil and fresh/potable water systems) -- candidates who give general contamination discussion instead of naming the systems lose marks there, though parts (b) and (c) (conditions for bacterial growth, detection methods) are usually handled well.

canonical_answers.title: Auxiliary Diesel Engine LO Sample Results — Causes and Greatest Concern
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(i) High acidity.** Oxidation/degradation of the oil (overheating, aeration, old oil); acidic combustion products from fuel sulphur blowing past the pistons, depleting alkalinity (TBN).

**(ii) High sediment content.** Wear debris and carbon/oxidation products from normal/abnormal wear; dirt ingress and additive breakdown, plus a failing purifier or filter.

**(iii) Excessive water content.** Cooling-water leakage into the crankcase (leaking liner seals, cooler tubes); condensation from cool/intermittent operation or purifier malfunction.

**(iv) Fuel dilution.** Leaking fuel injection equipment (dripping injectors, HP pump glands); poor/incomplete combustion (faulty atomisation, prolonged idling).

**(b) Greatest concern.** Excessive water content (iii) generally gives the greatest concern — it promotes rapid corrosion, destroys the lubricating film and can lead to bearing wipe/failure, accelerates oil degradation, and if from a cooling-water leak signals a developing mechanical defect that will worsen.
examiner_focus: A straightforward recall question, but candidates should aim to give TWO plausible causes for each LO sample result (e.g. high acidity: oxidation, acidic combustion products; high sediment: dirty fuel, wear debris; excessive water: cooler leak, condensation; fuel dilution: injector/pump leakage, incomplete combustion) rather than a single cause each, to maximise the available marks.

canonical_answers.title: Modern Shaft Torsion Meter; Torque/Speed & Hull Efficiency
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw a split-ring/collar clamped around the shaft carrying four strain gauges bonded at 45° to the axis, connected as a Wheatstone bridge. Show a stationary pickup reading the rotating collar (inductive coupling or telemetry), feeding a display unit.*

**Principle.** When the shaft transmits torque, it twists, producing shear stress that manifests as principal tensile and compressive strains at 45° to the shaft axis. Four strain gauges bonded at 45° form a full Wheatstone bridge — two sensing tension, two compression — giving doubled sensitivity, automatic temperature compensation, and cancellation of bending/axial thrust strains so the bridge responds to torsion only.

**Construction and operation.** As torque is applied, gauges in tension increase resistance and those in compression decrease, unbalancing the bridge; output voltage is directly proportional to torque. The gauges and bridge electronics are carried on a split-ring clamped around the shaft, signal transmitted across the rotating-to-stationary gap by inductive (rotary transformer) coupling or radio telemetry — no slip rings in modern meters. The stationary pickup also incorporates a speed sensor. The display shows torque, speed, and shaft power computed as P = 2πNT.

**(b) Importance for hull efficiency.** Under MARPOL Annex VI, EEDI and SEEMP require ships to demonstrate and continually improve energy efficiency. Shaft torque and speed give delivered shaft power (P = 2πNT); comparing this against ship speed and baseline (sea trial) data quantifies true propulsive efficiency. A rise in torque/power for the same ship speed reveals hull or propeller fouling, enabling informed decisions on hull cleaning and voyage optimisation.
examiner_focus: A low-attempt question when new, but once established, the strain-gauge/optical/magnetic torsion-meter principle is well handled; part (b) is where marks slip -- few candidates connect torque/speed monitoring to exhaust emissions performance or the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI), which is the real-world reason it matters.

canonical_answers.title: Propeller Slip — Definition, Calculation & Affecting Conditions
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** Propeller slip is the difference between the theoretical distance the propeller should advance (pitch × revolutions) and the actual distance the ship travels, expressed as a percentage of the theoretical distance: Slip% = [(P×N − V×t) / (P×N)] × 100.

**(b) Four conditions affecting slip, with reasons**
1. Hull fouling/increased roughness — increases resistance, so actual distance falls for the same revolutions, increasing slip.
2. Weather and sea conditions — head wind/seas increase resistance and reduce propeller efficiency (propeller racing near the surface), increasing slip; a following sea can reduce or reverse it.
3. Draught, trim and displacement — a deeply laden ship has greater resistance, reducing speed for given RPM; in ballast the propeller may ventilate, losing thrust and increasing slip.
4. Propeller surface condition/damage — fouling, roughness or cavitation erosion disturbs flow over the blades, reducing efficiency and increasing slip even with unchanged revolutions and pitch.
examiner_focus: Part (a) (define slip) causes the most trouble despite being worth only 2 marks. Part (b) demands FOUR conditions WITH REASONS -- a bare word like 'fouling' or 'bad weather' earns nothing without explaining the mechanism (e.g. fouling increases resistance so the propeller can't achieve its theoretical advance speed at the same rpm).

canonical_answers.title: Air-Type Radial Lip Stern Tube Seal (Pollution Prevention)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw an aft seal with lip seals #1-#3 facing aft (seawater) and forward (oil), separated by a pressurised air chamber, an air control unit feeding the chamber, a forward seal tank, LO tank and a drain tank monitoring leakage.*

An air-type (void space) seal interposes a pressurised air chamber between the seawater seals and the oil seals, so oil and seawater are never in direct contact across a single lip.

**Air supply.** Control air is fed continuously into the void space at a small constant flow (~40–50 L/min), the regulator maintaining pressure slightly above ambient seawater pressure, following draught changes.

**Pollution prevention.** Since chamber pressure slightly exceeds sea pressure, any leakage across the aft lip seals is a harmless trickle of air bubbling outward — not oil; seawater cannot pass inward against the air pressure.

**Drain/monitoring.** The bottom of the air chamber connects to a drain tank in the engine room with a sight/level alarm: water indicates aft seawater-seal wear, oil indicates aft oil-seal wear — giving early warning without pollution occurring.
examiner_focus: Reasonably well answered -- no strong recurring trap noted for this occurrence.

canonical_answers.title: Power Transmission Through Shafting; Coupling Bolt Stresses; Hydraulic Bolt Sketch
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) How power is transmitted.** Power is a function of torque and rotational speed (P=2πNT); the shafting transmits the engine's torque to the propeller at essentially steady speed. Shaft sections are joined by flanged couplings, torque passing across each joint by friction grip between clamped flange faces (the primary mechanism with hydraulic bolts) and/or shear/bearing of accurately fitted coupling bolts. Propeller thrust is taken out separately at the thrust block.

**(b) Three operational factors inducing high bolt stress**
1. Torsional vibration/torque fluctuations — cyclic engine firing torque, especially near a barred speed range.
2. Shock torque loadings — propeller striking ice/debris, racing in heavy weather, crash-astern manoeuvres.
3. Shaft misalignment — bearing wear-down or hull deflections bending the shaft each revolution.

**(c) Hydraulic coupling bolt sketch.**
*Sketch instructions: draw two flanges with a hollow bolt through a reamed hole, a nut, a hydraulic jack screwed onto the bolt head with a piston and oil connection.*

The hydraulic jack stretches the bolt elastically with high-pressure oil; the nut is run down hand-tight while stretched; releasing pressure leaves the bolt under accurate pre-tension, clamping the flanges so torque transmits by friction.
examiner_focus: Part (a) is the trap: candidates describe combustion/piston/crankshaft mechanics ending at the thrust block, when the question is specifically about POWER TRANSMISSION THROUGH THE SHAFTING -- power is torque x speed, transmitted at steady rotational speed through the couplings, not about how the power was generated. Parts (b)-(c) are handled well, with either a sleeved or hollow hydraulic bolt sketch accepted.

canonical_answers.title: Combination Seal: Wrapped Bellows Face Seal + Lip Seal
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw rotating/stationary flat annular faces (mechanical seal) outboard, a wrapped bellows/spring assembly pressing them together, a lip seal inboard, a void space between them draining to a leakage tank, and a rope guard outboard.*

This combination seal places two sealing principles in series: a radial face seal (mechanical seal) as the primary seawater seal outboard, and a radial lip seal as the primary oil seal inboard, with a monitored void space between.

**The radial face seal.** Two optically flat annular faces rub at right angles to the shaft axis; the rotating face turns with the shaft, the stationary face is fixed to the sternframe. The wrapped bellows/spring presses the faces together, accommodates axial movement and wear, and forms the static seal and drive without a sliding static joint.

**The lip seal.** Inboard of the void space, a radial lip seal retains stern tube lubricating oil, its lip pressed onto the liner by the oil's static head.

**The void space.** Drained to a leakage tank: seawater passing the face seal drains harmlessly inboard; oil weeping past the lip seal collects in the same tank rather than reaching the sea. Monitoring the tank's contents (oil or water) reveals which seal is deteriorating.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the mark-earning distinction is that this combination seal pairs a wrapped bellows RADIAL FACE seal (for the primary oil-side sealing, self-adjusting via the bellows) with a conventional lip seal as a secondary/backup barrier -- both elements need to appear in the sketch and description.

canonical_answers.title: Muff (SKF OK) Type Propeller Shaft Coupling
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw two plain shaft ends butted together, a thin tapered inner sleeve spanning both, an alloy steel outer sleeve with matching taper fitted over it, a nut and seal ring forming a hydraulic jack, and press-up distance reference marks.*

**(b) Connection.** The plain shaft ends are aligned and butted; the tapered inner sleeve is positioned to span both equally, with the outer sleeve fitted over it. A clamping nut with seal ring forms an annular hydraulic jack; press-up oil pressure between nut and outer sleeve draws the outer sleeve up the taper of the inner sleeve, compressing the thin inner sleeve radially onto both shaft ends — torque is transmitted by friction grip alone, no keys or bolts. The press-up distance against reference marks confirms the designed grip. Separation oil is injected between the tapers during fitting to float the sleeves for smooth movement.
examiner_focus: Low attempt numbers; sketches of the muff coupling tend to be good but the description of HOW it's connected (heating/expanding the muff sleeve to slide over both shaft ends, or hydraulically expanding it, then allowing it to shrink and grip) is consistently too brief.

canonical_answers.title: Tilting Pad Shaft (Journal) Support Bearing
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
This is a tilting pad JOURNAL (shaft support) bearing, not the Michell thrust bearing — the sketch must show a radial arrangement.

*Sketch instructions: draw a shaft supported by three separate pivoted pads around the lower half of the journal, each with its own lobed pressure profile shown as a dashed curve rising from the leading edge, peaking near the trailing edge, and falling to zero at the pad exit.*

**(a) Operation.** As the shaft rotates, oil is dragged toward the leading edge of each pad; being free to pivot, the pad tilts to form a convergent wedge-shaped oil gap. Oil drawn into the wedge generates hydrodynamic pressure that lifts and supports the shaft with full fluid-film lubrication. Each pad develops its own pressure wedge; the shaft is supported by several separate pressure peaks rather than one single hump. Each pad is mounted on a spherical seat, letting it align axially with shaft slope or deflection.

**(b) Why evolved — advantages.** Multiple pads increase the number of oil wedges, giving greater overall load-carrying capacity, allowing shorter bearings and greater spacing. The self-adjusting tilt accommodates alignment changes from hull deflection or wear-down that a rigid plain bush cannot follow without edge-loading. Load distribution across pads reduces maximum oil film temperature per pad.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the mark-earning point for tilting-pad bearings is that each pad can pivot to form its own optimal oil wedge angle regardless of load/speed changes, giving more even pressure distribution and better performance at varying loads than a plain fixed-profile bearing -- that adaptability, not just 'more oil film,' is the advantage to state.

canonical_answers.title: Keyless Propeller — Hydraulic (Wet) Fit & Withdrawal
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
This is the oil injection (wet) fit — not the Pilgrim nut dry fit and not a muff coupling.

*Sketch instructions: draw the tapered tail shaft, propeller hub with injection points connected to high-pressure hoses, a hydraulic nut, and a dial gauge measuring push-up.*

**(a)** The propeller boss has a plain tapered bore with circumferential oil distribution grooves fed through radial drillings. The propeller is pushed onto the taper to a firm seating; a hydraulic nut is fitted behind the hub. High-pressure oil injected into the grooves at the taper interface floats the hub on a pressurised oil film, almost eliminating friction. Oil pressure to the hydraulic nut then advances the propeller axially up the taper to a specified push-up distance on the dial gauge. The injection oil is released first (boss grips the cone with full designed interference), then the hydraulic nut pressure.

**(b) Two advantages vs dry fit.** No heating required, accurate repeatable grip achieved cold; easy controlled removal by re-injecting oil to float the joint, without heat or heavy pulling gear.

**(c) How thrust is transmitted.** Purely by friction: the push-up leaves the boss stretched elastically around the shaft cone, producing high radial contact pressure whose product with contact area and coefficient of friction gives a friction force far exceeding that needed to transmit torque and thrust with a safety margin.
examiner_focus: A question that reliably splits into three answer types: only a minority correctly describe the hydraulic WET fit and withdrawal method being asked for; a large number instead describe a DRY fit (some even depicting the pilgrim nut in withdrawal mode, which belongs to the dry-fit method); and some go completely off-track describing a muff coupling, which isn't a propeller-fitting method at all.

canonical_answers.title: Tunnel Type Bow Thrusters — Multiple Units; Prime Movers & Transmission
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why more than one thruster.** Greater total thrust requirement — large vessels with high windage need more side thrust than one practicable tunnel can deliver. Redundancy and operational availability — ships depending on thrusters for berthing without tugs fit multiple units so one failure doesn't prevent safe manoeuvring.

**(b) Prime mover and transmission options**
1. Electric motor drive (most common) — a constant-speed AC motor drives the impeller through bevel gears, either with a Controllable Pitch Propeller (fast, stepless response) or a variable-speed drive with Fixed Pitch Propeller (simpler, robust propeller, costly converter).
2. Hydraulic motor drive — a power pack supplies a hydraulic motor at the tunnel unit; stepless reversible control, but lower transmission efficiency and more maintenance.
3. Direct diesel engine drive — a dedicated diesel drives the unit through a clutch, independent of the ship's electrical load, but with engine maintenance and slower response.
examiner_focus: The least popular question in the topic, but scores well among the few who attempt it -- suggesting bow-thruster prime-mover/transmission options (electric motor, hydraulic motor, direct diesel drive; right-angle gear vs L-drive) are a well-understood but under-revised area.

canonical_answers.title: Hydraulic Jacking to Check Bearing Loads; Load/Lift Graph
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Method.** A calibrated hydraulic jack is placed under the shaft close to the bearing; a dial gauge on the bearing housing reads shaft lift. Oil pressure is applied in increments, recording jack load and lift at each step; once the shaft lifts clear (limited to ~0.5mm, not until it touches the top of the bearing), the relationship becomes a straight line. The pressure is then released in increments, recording readings on the way down as well — friction gives a hysteresis loop between raising and lowering curves. The test is repeated at a defined ship condition.

**(b) The graph.**
*Sketch instructions: plot shaft lift (mm, vertical) against jack load (bar, horizontal). Draw a raising curve (initially flat/curved, becoming straight once the shaft lifts clear) and a lowering curve lying to the left of it due to jack friction. Extrapolate the straight portions of both back to zero lift, and draw the mean line between the two intercepts.*

The mean of the two straight-line extrapolations to zero lift gives the true jack load at which the bearing is just unloaded (friction errors cancelling); multiplied by a jack-position correction factor, this gives the bearing load.
examiner_focus: Part (a) has a specific recurring gap: candidates forget that the shaft is jacked in BOTH directions -- raised AND lowered -- with both sets of readings recorded and plotted, not just jacked up until contact with the top of the bearing.

canonical_answers.title: Stern Tube Bearings: White Metal Failure; Merits of Non-Metallic Bearings
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why white metal is susceptible to failure.** Edge loading from the overhung propeller concentrates load at the aft bearing end. Low melting point/poor high-temperature strength means any oil-film loss (slow turning, loss of lubrication) causes wiping. Dependence on a perfect hydrodynamic film means low RPM (turning gear, slow steaming) risks boundary contact and damage. Water contamination from seal wear destroys the film and corrodes the white metal. Fatigue and bonding failure from cyclic loading can crack the lining.

**(b) Merits of non-metallic bearings.** Seawater lubrication — zero oil pollution, no oil seal to fail. Tolerance of contamination and poor lubrication — resilient polymer surfaces allow abrasive particles to embed/pass without seizure. Resilience and vibration damping — conforms to slight misalignment. Simplicity and reduced maintenance — no oil system, header tanks or oil analysis. Corrosion immunity — the material itself does not corrode in seawater.
examiner_focus: A question that should be straightforward (why white-metal fails, merits of non-metallic bearings) but has produced consistently mixed-to-poor results across sittings, described by one examiner's report as 'mystifying' given its recurrence.

canonical_answers.title: Hydraulic Coupling Bolt — Sketch, Advantages, Stresses
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** As per Q4's sketch above.

**(b) Advantages compared to conventional bolts.** Accurate, repeatable pre-tension set directly by hydraulic pressure × piston area, evenly shared around the flange. No torsional or surface damage during tightening (bolt stretched axially, not twisted). Quick, easy and safe fitting/removal even after years in service — no drifts or flame cutting of seized bolts.

**(c)** As per Q4's three factors above (torsional vibration, shock torque loadings, shaft misalignment).
examiner_focus: Sketch quality is the specific mark-loser here -- several candidates produce sketches too poor or unworkable to earn credit for the hydraulic coupling bolt, even when the advantages/stress-factor parts are answered fine.

canonical_answers.title: Shaft Alignment Check Without Removing Coupling Bolts; Misalignment Effects
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) The bearing load (jack-up) method.** With couplings still bolted, alignment is verified by measuring the load each bearing carries and comparing with the calculated design value — as per Q10's jacking method, taken at each bearing in turn and compared against the alignment calculation.

**(b) Why check afloat in light ship condition.** The alignment must be verified in the condition for which it was calculated, with representative hull deflections: afloat (dry dock blocking distorts the hull), light ship giving the reference condition typically representing the worst case for alignment.

**(c)(i) Effect on coupling bolts.** The bend rotates with each revolution, subjecting the bolts to cyclic bending/tensile stress superimposed on pre-tension — leading to fatigue failure.

**(c)(ii) Effect on shaft bearings.** The shaft bears hard on the edges of individual bearings (edge loading), overloading some and unloading others, causing overheating and wiping.

**(d) Greatest concern.** The effect on coupling bolts is of greater concern — bearing damage develops progressively and reveals itself through rising temperatures, but bolt fatigue is cumulative, hidden and gives no warning; sudden fracture could part the coupling at sea with complete loss of propulsion.
examiner_focus: Part (a) catches some candidates describing CRANKSHAFT deflection checks instead of the main transmission SHAFT alignment method actually asked for -- these are different procedures on different components.

canonical_answers.title: Power Transmission & Improved Coupling Bolt Design
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** As per Q4's power transmission explanation above.

**(b) Four operational factors**
1. Torsional vibration/torque fluctuations.
2. Shock torque loadings (ice, debris, crash-astern).
3. Propeller racing in heavy weather (repeated emergence/re-immersion).
4. Shaft misalignment (bearing wear-down, hull deflections).

**(c) Improved design sketch.** The hydraulically tensioned coupling bolt (as per Q4/Q12), tensioned by stretching hydraulically rather than by torque or flogging, giving accurate even pre-tension with no torsional stress and easy removal. (The older centre-rod type — a hollow bolt with a central rod heated/stretched to tension it — is also acceptable.)
examiner_focus: Part (c) sketch quality is the weak point -- both the sleeved bolt and the older centre-rod design were accepted, but several sketches were unworkable or too poor to identify which design was intended.

canonical_answers.title: Podded Propulsion (360°): Advantages & Suited Vessel Types
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Advantages over conventional shafting/steering**
Superior manoeuvrability — full thrust directed through any angle, no reliance on a rudder deflecting the race.
Elimination of shafting, rudder and stern gear — no line shafting, stern tube sealing or rudder maintenance.
Space and design freedom — propulsion motor outside the hull frees machinery space.
Improved hydrodynamic efficiency — the pod propeller works in a clean wake, reducing appendage drag.
Reduced noise and vibration — no gearbox, even wake inflow.
Redundancy and operational flexibility with electric drive.

**(b) Vessel types most suited**
Cruise ships/large passenger vessels — already diesel-electric, need manoeuvrability and low noise.
Icebreakers/ice-class vessels — can direct full thrust in any direction and run astern-first through ice.
Ferries on tight schedules — frequent berthing without tugs.
DP vessels (offshore support, drill ships) — rapidly variable thrust in any direction for station-keeping.
examiner_focus: Generally well attempted, but a recurring digression is candidates going off-topic to describe Controllable Pitch Propeller (CPP) systems, or describing the PROPELLER on a fixed shaft rotating 360 degrees -- podded propulsion means the whole propulsion pod (motor plus propeller) rotates, not just the blades or a CPP hub.

canonical_answers.title: Propeller Cavitation: Definition & Detrimental Effects
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Definition.** Cavitation is the formation and subsequent collapse of vapour-filled cavities in the water at the propeller blades. Regions of high-velocity flow (chiefly on the suction face) experience a local pressure drop; where pressure falls below the water's vapour pressure, vapour cavities form, then collapse violently when carried into higher-pressure regions.

**(b) Four detrimental effects**
1. Erosion of blade material — cavity collapse produces intense local impact pressures, hammering the surface and tearing out particles, leaving spongy, pitted erosion.
2. Loss of thrust and efficiency — a vapour sheet blankets part of the blade, limiting lift; thrust breaks down while revolutions remain, slip increases and fuel consumption rises.
3. Noise and vibration — broadband underwater noise and fluctuating pressure impulses exciting hull and aft-end vibration.
4. Damage to adjacent components — rudder, stern frame and A-brackets suffer erosion; bent/eroded blades unbalance the propeller, accelerating stern tube bearing/seal wear.
examiner_focus: Consistently good answers -- no recurring trap noted for this occurrence.

canonical_answers.title: Podded vs Azimuthing Thrusters; Pusher/Tractor; Tandem Pods
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Both pods and azimuthing thrusters steer through 360° — neither is fixed. The true distinction is where the motor is and how drive is transmitted.

**(a)** Azimuthing thruster — prime mover inside the hull, power transmitted mechanically down a steerable leg via shafts and bevel gears (Z-drive or L-drive); power limited by gear capacity. Podded thruster — the propulsion motor is inside the submerged pod itself, coupled directly to the propeller shaft, no gearing; only electrical power passes down through the slewing arrangement, permitting much higher power and efficiency.

**(b) Thruster (pusher) vs tractor.** Pusher — propeller at the aft end, working in the wake of the pod body. Tractor — propeller at the forward end, pulling the unit, meeting clean water ahead of the pod. Advantage of tractor: undisturbed inflow gives higher efficiency and reduced cavitation/vibration/noise.

**(c) Tandem podded thrusters.** A tandem pod carries two propellers — one pulling forward, one pushing aft — on the same pod, sharing total power/thrust so each is more lightly loaded, allowing greater total power on one unit with reduced cavitation.
examiner_focus: Reasonably well answered, but a specific misconception recurs: candidates state that podded thrusters are FIXED/non-steerable, when steerability (360 degrees, like an azimuthing thruster) is actually one of their defining features -- the real distinction from azimuthing thrusters is where the prime mover sits (inside the pod vs inside the hull with mechanical drive down the leg).

canonical_answers.title: Shaft Alignment: Objectives, Conditions & Fair Curve Alignment
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Objectives.** To distribute the total shafting weight among all bearings so each carries an acceptable load. To keep bending stresses and cyclic stresses at couplings within safe limits, avoiding fatigue. To ensure these conditions are maintained throughout the range of service conditions (loaded/ballast, hot/cold, hull deflections).

**(b) Conditions to be met.** Each bearing must carry load within its permissible band (no unloaded or overloaded bearings). Relative slope between shaft and bearing must be acceptable, particularly at the aft stern tube bearing. Alignment must remain acceptable under all operating conditions (hull deflections, thermal rise, wear-down).

**(c) Fair curve alignment.** A loaded shaft naturally deflects into a smooth elastic curve under its own weight and the overhung propeller. Fair curve alignment is the modern method that accepts this curvature: the shafting is treated as a continuous elastic beam, and calculation determines the vertical offset at which each bearing must be set so the shaft, resting on all bearings, lies along its natural deflected curve — each bearing carrying its intended load share, with acceptable bending stresses throughout.
examiner_focus: Poorly answered overall. Part (a) is mostly missed because candidates describe the EFFECTS OF MISALIGNMENT instead of the actual OBJECTIVES of satisfactory alignment (even bearing load distribution, avoiding excessive bending stress, maintaining acceptable bearing reaction margins). Part (c) (fair curve alignment) is very weakly understood -- most candidates just describe the jacking arrangement used to measure bearing loads without explaining the fair-curve CONCEPT itself (the shaft forming a smooth, gently curving line through all bearings under its own weight and thermal/hull-deflection conditions, rather than a straight line).

canonical_answers.title: Chief Engineer's Report — Stern Tube Oil Loss to Sea
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
The oil is stated to have gone TO SEA — this is a pollution incident with statutory reporting obligations. Claiming "it went to the bilge instead" scores zero; the answer must show both the practical engineering response and reporting knowledge.

**Model report structure:**
**1. Incident summary** — header tank level fall identified, soundings confirming loss to sea via the aft seal, no abnormal bearing temperatures, slight sheen observed.
**2. Immediate actions taken** — Master informed immediately; SOPEP/SMPEP pollution report transmitted to coastal State, flag Administration, Company (DPA); Oil Record Book Part I entry recording the discharge, signed by Chief Engineer and Master; header tank gravity head reduced to the minimum safe value to lower differential pressure and stem leakage; shaft RPM reduced; leakage rate assessed by hourly soundings; void space drained and checked to identify the failing seal; oil samples drawn for analysis; spare/standby seal ring activated where the design permits.
**3. Cause (preliminary)** — wear/damage of the aft seal lip rings, possibly aggravated by fishing line debris; confirmation requires diver inspection.
**4. Recommendations** — diver inspection and seal renewal at next port; replenishment of stern tube oil and consideration of an Environmentally Acceptable Lubricant (EAL); Class advised as applicable; SMS non-conformity report for fleet circulation.
examiner_focus: A cautionary pattern across repeat sittings: many candidates take the path of least resistance and answer as if the oil stayed in the bilge (no pollution, no real incident to report), even when the question explicitly states the oil was lost TO SEA -- doing so scores zero regardless of how well-written the rest of the report is, since it ignores the actual pollution incident the question describes.

canonical_answers.title: Outboard Radial Lip Seal: Sketch & In-Situ Replacement (Vulcanising)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw the shaft with a chrome-steel/ceramic-coated liner, a seal housing bolted to the stern frame in split casing rings, four radial lip seal rings (#0-#3) with outer rings facing aft (seawater) and inner rings facing forward (oil), each pressed onto the liner by a garter spring.*

**(b) Replacing the seal without removing the tail shaft.** Access is gained in dry dock, or afloat by trimming/heeling to bring the seal clear, or using divers with a cofferdam. The header tank is drained down, the rope guard removed, and the shaft locked against turning. The split casing rings are unbolted to expose the old seal rings, which are cut through and removed; the liner is inspected for grooving.

**The key point:** since the shaft remains in place, a new endless seal ring cannot be slid over the propeller. Each new seal ring is supplied as an open ring, wrapped around the liner, and its ends joined in situ by hot vulcanising (bonding) — scarf-cut ends, bonding solution applied, clamped in a heated press at the specified temperature and time, then dressed smooth to restore an endless ring.

The bonded ring is seated with its garter spring, the split casing rings re-assembled, and the assembly pressure/leak tested before the header tank is refilled and the rope guard refitted.
examiner_focus: Part (a) (sketch) is reliably strong, typically scoring 4-5 of the 5 marks; part (b) is weak -- candidates give generic stock answers rather than actually describing the in-situ replacement PROCEDURE, in particular the vulcanising (or equivalent) process that allows a new seal to be fitted and bonded without drawing the tail shaft.

canonical_answers.title: Fully Automatic DX System — LP Switch & HP Switch Faults
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw two rooms (e.g. meat room and veg room) each with a solenoid valve and TEV, a back pressure valve on the warmer room's suction, LP/HP switches sensing compressor suction and discharge, an oil separator, condenser with relief valve, drier and sight glass. Annotate room temperatures (e.g. meat room −10°C, veg room +4°C).*

**(b) LP switch operation.** The LP switch senses compressor suction pressure and provides automatic start/stop control. When all room thermostats are satisfied, their solenoids close, the compressor pumps down the low side, and suction pressure falls; at the cut-out setting the switch opens and stops the compressor. When a room warms up, its solenoid re-opens, suction pressure rises, and at the cut-in setting the switch closes and restarts the compressor. The differential between cut-in and cut-out prevents short cycling.

**(c) Two faults causing the HP switch to operate, with reasons**
Loss of condenser cooling water (failed pump, blocked suction) — heat of condensation cannot be rejected, so discharge pressure rises rapidly.
Fouled/scaled condenser tubes — reduced heat transfer raises condensing temperature and pressure.

Other acceptable: air/incondensable gases in the system; overcharge of refrigerant. Never say "faulty HP switch" — it must be a system fault.
examiner_focus: Strong sketches for part (a), but part (b) commonly stops halfway: candidates say the LP switch cuts the compressor OUT on falling pressure but omit that it also cuts back IN when pressure rises again -- both directions need stating. Part (c) needs reasons attached to each fault, and 'a faulty HP switch' is not itself an accepted answer -- it has to be an actual system fault (e.g. SW cooling failure, air in the condenser, overcharge) that causes the switch to trip.

canonical_answers.title: Undercooling & the Liquid–Suction Heat Exchanger
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Why undercooling is desirable.** Increased refrigerating effect — liquid enters the expansion valve with lower enthalpy, so less flashes to vapour, giving more liquid in the evaporator per kg circulated. Prevents flash gas in the liquid line. Ensures solid liquid reaches the expansion valve.

**(b) Liquid-suction heat exchanger.**
*Sketch instructions: draw warm liquid from the condenser outlet in counterflow against cold suction vapour from the evaporator outlet, in a shell-and-coil or tube-in-tube arrangement.*

Warm liquid leaving the condenser flows through one side; cold vapour leaving the evaporator flows through the other in counterflow. Heat transfers through the tube wall from liquid to vapour — true heat exchange, not flash cooling. The liquid is subcooled before the expansion valve; the suction vapour is superheated, protecting against liquid carry-over.

**Trap:** an open flash economiser is just a vessel with no heat-transfer surface (cooling by partial evaporation) — it is not a heat exchanger and scores nothing.

**(c) Consequences of a dryness fraction at compressor suction.** Liquid slugging/mechanical damage — incompressible liquid droplets can cause broken valve plates, damaged pistons. Loss of lubrication — liquid entering the crankcase washes oil from cylinder walls and dilutes the sump oil.
examiner_focus: Part (a) is handled well, sometimes using a graph to support the explanation. Part (b) is where most marks are lost: a genuine heat exchanger needs TWO separate fluid streams (one being heated, one being cooled) -- an arrangement using a second expansion valve/flash-off stage instead of a true two-flow heat exchanger doesn't meet the definition, and the heat exchanger must be positioned to use the cooler liquid line (not warm gas before the condenser) to subcool the warmer liquid leaving the condenser.

canonical_answers.title: Superheat & Undercooling on the Pressure–Enthalpy Diagram
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Why superheating is desirable.** Protects the compressor from liquid carry-over (no liquid slugging, no oil dilution). Confirms full use of the evaporator (all liquid evaporated). Enables TEV control, which regulates by maintaining a set degree of superheat.

**(a)(ii) Why undercooling is desirable.** Increased refrigerating effect (lower enthalpy at the expansion valve). Prevents flash gas in the liquid line. Ensures solid liquid at the expansion valve.

**(b) Effect on cooling load, with P-h diagram.**
*Sketch instructions: draw the basic cycle (1-2 compression, 2-3 condensation, 3-4 expansion at constant enthalpy, 4-1 evaporation). Show subcooling moving point 3 left to 3' (and 4 to 4' correspondingly), and superheat moving point 1 right to 1'.*

The refrigerating effect per kg is the width of the evaporation line (h1−h4). With subcooling, h4 falls, increasing the refrigerating effect with no increase in compressor work — a genuine COP gain. With useful superheat (gained within the cooled space), h1 rises, adding to the refrigerating effect; superheat gained outside the cooled space adds nothing useful, only increasing compressor work.
examiner_focus: Part (a) is fine, but part (b) exposes weak P-h diagram literacy -- many candidates can't sketch even a simple Pressure-Enthalpy diagram or connect superheat/undercooling to the resulting change in evaporator cooling load (extended vaporisation length / increased refrigerating effect), despite this being a frequently recurring question.

canonical_answers.title: Air Conditioning — Comfort Zone, NW Europe & Arabian Gulf, Recirculation (I)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Comfort zone boundaries.** Approximately 21°C to 27°C dry bulb, 30% to 70% RH, controlled toward the centre (~22–25°C, 50% RH).

**(b)(i) NW Europe winter.** Cold, low-moisture outside air is heated (dropping RH well below comfort band), then humidified (dry steam/water spray), then reheated as necessary.

**(b)(ii) Arabian Gulf summer.** Hot, very humid air is cooled below its dew point (dehumidification, condensate drains away), leaving the coil cool and near-saturated, then slightly reheated to bring RH down into the comfort band. *(Never say the air is humidified after cooling — it is already near-saturated.)*

**(c) Four locations where conditioned air must not be recirculated**
Galley — cooking odours, grease, smoke.
Sanitary spaces — offensive odours and bacteria.
Ship's hospital — infectious organisms.
Laundry/drying rooms — high moisture, lint, detergent fumes.
examiner_focus: Reasonably good overall; the main weak spot is sketch quality for the psychrometric/comfort-zone points rather than the written content.

canonical_answers.title: Purpose of Components — Thermostat, TEV, HP Cut-out, Safety Head, Unloader
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Room thermostat.** Senses room temperature and opens/closes the liquid-line solenoid valve to give automatic independent control of each room.

**(b) Expansion valve.** Reduces pressure from condenser to evaporator pressure at constant enthalpy, and regulates flow to maintain a set superheat at the evaporator outlet.

**(c) High pressure cut out.** A safety device sensing discharge pressure, stopping the compressor before a dangerous pressure ruptures a component; normally hand-reset.

**(d) Safety head.** Protects a reciprocating compressor against liquid slugging — the cylinder head/discharge valve seat is spring-loaded and lifts to relieve excessive pressure from a liquid slug, then re-seats automatically.

**(e) Unloader.** A capacity control device that holds cylinder suction valves open so those cylinders idle, matching compressor capacity to cooling demand in steps and reducing starting torque.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; a common trap in similar 'purpose of components' questions is describing HOW a component works rather than WHY it's fitted (its purpose) -- keep each answer to purpose/function, not full operating detail.

canonical_answers.title: Refrigerant Faults — Air, Oil, Moisture, Undercharge, Overcharge
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Air.** Indication: high discharge pressure (air's partial pressure adds to refrigerant pressure). Remedy: purge from the condenser top with cooling water running.

**(b) Oil.** Indication: reduced cooling effect (oil coats evaporator surfaces), falling sump level. Remedy: drain oil from evaporator, overhaul the discharge oil separator.

**(c) Moisture.** Indication: icing-up of the expansion valve (intermittent cooling, recovers when warmed). Remedy: renew the drier cartridge; in bad cases evacuate and recharge dry.

**(d) Undercharge.** Indication: bubbles in the sight glass, low suction/discharge pressures. Remedy: find and repair the leak first, then recharge.

**(e) Overcharge.** Indication: high discharge pressure (excess liquid floods condenser tubes), high receiver level. Remedy: remove excess charge to a recovery cylinder.
examiner_focus: Mostly well answered; the one flagged issue is candidates drifting toward fire-fighting/emergency response content rather than staying on refrigerant-fault indication and remedy, which is what the question actually asks for.

canonical_answers.title: Provision Plant Sketch & Sequence of Events on Demand
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** As per Q1's sketch, extended to multiple rooms with individual solenoid/TEV per room, back pressure valve, oil separator, drier and sight glass.

**(b) Sequence of events**
1. Room temperature rises above the thermostat set point.
2. The thermostat energises the solenoid valve, which opens.
3. Refrigerant flows through the TEV to the evaporator and boils, absorbing heat.
4. Suction pressure rises; at the LP switch's cut-in setting, the LP switch starts the compressor (not the thermostat directly).
5. Normal running — compressor draws vapour, compresses and discharges through the oil separator to the condenser; liquid passes via the drier and sight glass.
6. Room reaches desired temperature; the thermostat de-energises the solenoid, which closes.
7. Pump-down — the compressor continues, clearing refrigerant from the evaporator, until suction pressure reaches the LP cut-out and the compressor stops.
examiner_focus: The sketch in part (a) is usually good, but part (b) drifts into describing how the individual COMPONENTS work rather than the actual SEQUENCE OF EVENTS asked for. A specific, recurring error is stating the solenoid valve opens when room temperature FALLS (it's the opposite -- rising room temperature is what triggers the thermostat, opens the solenoid, and starts the sequence toward the compressor running) -- the answer needs to be a chronological story from rising temperature through to the room reaching its set point again.

canonical_answers.title: Comfort Zone Definition, Objectives & Recirculation (II)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Comfort zone.** The area on the psychrometric chart, bounded by temperature and RH limits, within which most people feel comfortable — the four boundary points approximately 21°C/30%RH, 21°C/70%RH, 27°C/30%RH, 27°C/70%RH.

**(b) Objectives, stated as positive aims.** Comfort, health and wellbeing of crew/passengers. Efficiency and safety of the crew (fatigue and heat stress degrade alertness). Protection of the accommodation and equipment (humidity limits preventing condensation/corrosion or excessive dryness).

**(c) Five areas not to recirculate, with reasons**
Galley, sanitary spaces, ship's hospital, laundry/drying rooms (as per Q4), plus pantries — food odours and heat from hot presses.

These must all be spaces that ARE supplied with conditioned air in the first place — machinery spaces, paint lockers, holds etc. are wrong answers since conditioned air is never sent there.
examiner_focus: A genuinely confused topic across sittings. Part (a) needs actual temperature/humidity VALUES at the comfort-zone boundary points, not just a description. Part (b) asks for the OBJECTIVES of staying in the comfort zone (occupant comfort, health, productivity) -- many candidates instead describe symptoms of getting it WRONG (dry throat, sweating, mould), which is the opposite of what's asked. Part (c) is a location question -- conditioned air is never supplied to machinery spaces, cargo holds, chain lockers or paint lockers in the first place, so naming those as 'recirculation exclusions' is wrong; the correct list is spaces like hospital/sick bay, galley and laundry, where air must not be recirculated back into the general system.

canonical_answers.title: AHU Block Diagram & Prevention of Bacterial Growth
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw a central AHU: outside air and recirculated air mixing at dampers, through a filter, over a cooling coil, past a heating coil and steam humidifier, driven by a supply fan through zone reheat coils to the conditioned spaces, with a return trunking loop. Annotate state points e.g. outside air 35°C/40%RH, recirculated air 23°C/55%RH, mixed air 28°C/48%RH, supply air 16°C/85%RH, delivered 23°C/55%RH.*

Annotating each state point and labelling every component is what scores full marks — an unannotated block diagram loses most of them.

**(b) Preventing bacterial growth.** Eliminate standing water — drain trays kept clear and self-draining. Use dry steam for humidification rather than water sprays, avoiding the warm-water reservoir bacteria colonise. Regular cleaning/renewal of filters and biocide treatment of coils/trays.
examiner_focus: Generally fine -- no strong recurring trap noted for this occurrence.

canonical_answers.title: DX System Sketch & FIVE Thermodynamic Properties of a Refrigerant
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Four plain boxes (compressor/condenser/expansion valve/evaporator) scores zero at management level. Full marks need LP/HP cut-outs, oil separator, condenser relief valve, drier, sight glass, solenoid + thermostat, TEV adjacent to its cold room, and annotated room temperatures.

**(b) Five thermodynamic properties, with reasons**
High latent heat of vaporisation — smaller mass flow for the required refrigerating effect.
Low specific volume of suction vapour — smaller compressor displacement for a given duty.
Evaporating pressure above atmospheric — leakage is outward and detectable, not inward (air/moisture ingress).
Moderate condensing pressure — lighter scantlings, less compression work.
Critical temperature well above condensing temperature — ensures the refrigerant can actually be condensed.

Trap: COP is a ratio (a result), not a thermodynamic property; "non-toxic/cheap/environmentally friendly" are desirable but not thermodynamic.
examiner_focus: The single worst-performing question in this topic, which is surprising for this level. Part (a): a bare four-box block diagram (compressor/condenser/expansion valve/evaporator) with no further system detail scores zero at management level -- proper componentry and annotation is expected. Part (b): candidates confuse a RATIO like Coefficient of Performance with an actual thermodynamic PROPERTY of the refrigerant itself (e.g. low boiling point, high latent heat of vaporisation, chemically stable/non-corrosive, non-toxic/non-flammable, compatible with lubricants) -- COP is not a valid answer here.

canonical_answers.title: Compressor Lubrication — Synthetic Oils, Carry-over, Oil Separator
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Advantage of fully synthetic oils.** Excellent miscibility with modern refrigerants and chemical stability across the working temperature range; very low wax content and pour point, so they don't deposit wax in cold parts of the system as mineral oils can.

**(b) Why oil is carried over.** Normal cylinder lubrication mist swept out with discharge gas; refrigerant dissolved in crankcase oil boiling out on start-up (oil foaming); mechanical wear or overfilling.

**(c) Oil separator.** A vessel in the discharge line: hot gas enters and impinges on baffle plates, the velocity drop and direction change throwing oil droplets out of the gas stream; oil collects at the bottom, and a float-operated needle valve returns it to the crankcase using the discharge-to-suction pressure difference, while cleaned gas continues to the condenser.

**(d) Two reasons oil accumulation in the evaporator is undesirable.** Reduced heat transfer (insulating film on tubes). Loss of compressor lubrication (oil missing from the sump risks bearing wear/seizure).
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; part (c) (device returning oil to the sump) should describe an actual oil separator (gas velocity reduced, oil droplets coalesce and drain back via a float-controlled return line), not just 'an oil separator is fitted' without describing its operating principle.

canonical_answers.title: Comfort Zone Boundary Points (Trott & Welch) & Location Control
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Boundary points (per Trott & Welch).** Approximately 18°C at 72% RH, 22°C at 32% RH, 24°C at 72% RH, and 27°C at 32% RH — the envelope sloping so a lower temperature is needed for comfort at higher humidity.

**(b)(i) NW Europe winter.** Minimum fresh air mixed with warm recirculated air to conserve heat; the mixed air is heated, humidified with dry steam, and reheated as required.

**(b)(ii) Arabian Gulf summer.** Hot, humid outside air mixed with recirculated air (already ~23°C/55%RH); cooled below dew point (dehumidification), then reheated to the supply condition — no humidification needed since the air already holds ample moisture.
examiner_focus: The comfort-zone boundary VALUES are treated flexibly by examiners (Trott & Welch's approximate points, or reasonable equivalents, are accepted) since interpretations vary across textbooks -- the bigger mark-loser is part (b), where candidates rarely mention that recirculated air needs managing, or that Arabian Gulf summer air is markedly HUMID as well as hot, which affects how the comfort zone is maintained.

canonical_answers.title: Fault Diagnosis — Pressure, Cycling, Cooling Failure, Noise
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Excessive pressure.** Loss of condenser cooling water — restore flow. Air/incondensable gases — purge from the condenser.

**(b) Low suction pressure.** Undercharge (leak) — repair and recharge. Restricted/blocked expansion valve or drier (icing, dirt) — renew drier, clean valve.

**(c) Compressor cycling.** Undercharge — repair leak, recharge. LP switch differential too narrow — widen the cut-in/cut-out differential.

**(d) Running long but not cooling.** Evaporator heavily frosted/iced (insulating the coil) — defrost. Oil accumulated in the evaporator — drain oil, overhaul the oil separator.

**(e) Noisy operation.** Liquid/oil slugging — throttle the suction valve, correct the TEV setting/overcharge. Worn bearings/gudgeon pins/big ends — overhaul the compressor.
examiner_focus: A popular, well-scored question -- no recurring trap noted for this occurrence.

canonical_answers.title: AC Faults — Trunking, Drains, Capacity Control & Legionnaires' Disease
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Corroded return air trunking.** Ambient air (e.g. from a machinery space the trunking passes through) leaks in and dilutes the return air, altering its temperature/humidity; the plant must then work harder, increasing load and losing control of the conditioned space.

**(a)(ii) Blocked evaporator drains.** Condensate cannot drain, so the tray floods: water carries over into the supply air, and stagnant standing water becomes a breeding ground for Legionella.

**(a)(iii) Defective capacity control.** The plant can no longer modulate output to match load — either overcooling with short-cycling, or failing to meet demand on a hot day, so the spaces drift outside the comfort zone.

**(b) Main health hazard.** Legionnaires' disease, caused by Legionella pneumophila inhaled in aerosolised water droplets. Conditions required: stagnant water; warm temperature (~20–45°C); a nutrient source (sludge, scale, debris); and a means of aerosolising the water. Prevention: eliminate standing water; keep the system clean and disinfected; use dry steam rather than water-spray humidification; periodic biocide treatment.
examiner_focus: Part (a)(i) produces some very wide-of-the-mark answers -- corroded return-air trunking allowing rust into the system gets linked to implausible health effects (choking, oxygen depletion, CO2 formation) rather than the actual mechanism: the correct answer is that the fault lets ambient (unconditioned) air leak INTO the return duct, diluting the conditioned air and reducing the system's effective cooling/dehumidifying capacity -- and even candidates who identify the dilution effect often fail to follow through to what that does to the plant's performance.

canonical_answers.title: Steering Gear Checks on Taking Over a Vessel Without Handover
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**1. Documentation and records review.** Maker's manuals and schematics; Class certificates and survey status; planned maintenance records and defect history; steering gear test logbook; spare parts inventory verified against actual stock; confirm operating/changeover instructions posted on the bridge and steering flat (SOLAS requirement).

**2. Steering flat — visual inspection.** Cleanliness, lighting, access/escape routes; communications between bridge and steering flat tested; check for oil leaks at rams, glands and hoses; security of foundations and absence of corrosion.

**3. Hydraulic system.** Oil level in reservoirs and replenishment tank (capable of recharging at least one system, with low-level alarm); take an oil sample for analysis since condition history is unknown; filter condition; verify relief/shock valve settings against maker's figures; position of isolating valves.

**4. Power units, pumps and electrical supply.** Confirm two power units; megger test the motor windings; two separate supply circuits plus emergency source connection; verify motor protection (short-circuit, overload/loss-of-phase alarms, no automatic overload trip); running indicators and power-failure alarms on the bridge.

**5. Operational tests (SOLAS).** Main gear 35°-35° (and 35°-30°) in ≤28 seconds; auxiliary 15°-15° in ≤60 seconds; test all remote controls and changeover procedures; check rudder angle indicators; test emergency power supply.

**6. Alarms and emergency arrangements.** Test low oil level, low pressure, hydraulic lock and power-failure alarms; verify automatic isolating arrangements; carry out an emergency steering drill.

**7. Crew familiarisation.** Brief and drill watchkeepers and engineers on the layout, changeover and emergency operation, since none of the present crew has prior knowledge of this installation.

**Key idea:** "no handover" means independent verification (oil sampling, megger tests, checking actual valve settings and spares) rather than relying on records alone.
examiner_focus: Well answered in most sittings -- no recurring trap noted for this occurrence.

canonical_answers.title: Steering Gear Regulations; Pipe Coupling Failure & Single Failure Concept
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)(i) Rudder angle and time.** Main gear: 35° one side to 35° the other, and 35° to 30°, in not more than 28 seconds at deepest draught and maximum ahead service speed. Auxiliary: 15° to 15° in not more than 60 seconds, at deepest draught and half maximum ahead service speed or 7 knots, whichever is greater.

**(a)(ii) Electrical supply.** Two exclusive circuits fed directly from the main switchboard (one may run via the emergency switchboard), run separately as far as practicable. Short-circuit protection and overload alarm for each circuit/motor (audible and visual, e.g. on the bridge); no automatic overload trip; loss-of-phase alarm; running indicators on the bridge and at the main machinery control position.

**(b)(i) Factors contributing to pipe coupling failure.** Vibration fatiguing the joint; pressure surges/shock loading from the rudder in heavy weather; corrosion; ageing seals/O-rings; incorrect assembly; wrong-specification materials; inadequate pipe support.

**(b)(ii) Single failure concept.** No single failure in the steering gear should result in total loss of steering capability. A failure (burst pipe, oil loss, one power unit failing) must be detectable and isolable, leaving the remaining components able to maintain steering. For tankers/gas carriers of 10,000 GT and up, steering capability must be regained within 45 seconds of a single failure, achieved through duplicated power units, isolatable piping, and low-level/low-pressure alarms.
examiner_focus: Part (a) loses marks when candidates give the regulation for only MAIN or only AUXILIARY steering, not both, as the question asks for both. Part (b) has a persistent misconception: the single failure concept is treated as applying only to a drop in hydraulic oil level, when it actually covers ANY single failure -- electrical, mechanical or hydraulic -- and part (b)(i) needs the factors EXPLAINED (mechanism), not just named.
