canonical_answers.title: Compensated Control System for an Active Fin Stabiliser
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Active fin stabilisers reduce roll by projecting fins into the water flow and tilting them to an angle of attack, generating a hydrodynamic lift that produces a righting moment. Because lift depends on the square of ship speed, the system is only effective when the ship is making way.

*Sketch instructions: draw a gyro unit (sensing roll) feeding a compensating unit (angle + rate + acceleration terms) to a comparator (demand vs actual fin position feedback), through an amplifier to a hydraulic unit (servo valve + ram), driving the fin, which acts on the ship in the seaway subject to wave disturbance, with the ship's resulting roll sensed again by the gyro (outer loop) and fin position fed back to the comparator (inner loop).*

A system responding only to roll angle is unsatisfactory — at maximum roll the ship is momentarily stationary and about to roll back on its own, so angle-only correction applies force at the wrong moment. The compensated (three-term) system combines roll angle, roll velocity (the main damping term) and roll acceleration (providing anticipatory lead to cancel system lags):

demanded fin angle ∝ (k1×roll angle) + (k2×roll velocity) + (k3×roll acceleration)

The demanded fin angle is compared with actual fin position feedback (inner loop); any error drives the hydraulic actuator to reposition the fin. The ship's resulting roll is sensed again by the gyro (outer/master loop), and the cycle repeats. The unit also includes a fin-angle limiter, speed compensation, and provision for manual control and fin housing in harbour.
examiner_focus: A fair number of candidates sketch only a basic block diagram without the COMPENSATED element the question specifically asks for. The mark-earning structure is: Helm transmitter, roll acceleration sensor, roll velocity sensor, roll angle sensor and natural-list correction, all feeding into a summation unit -- a diagram missing the summation/compensation stage is marked down even if the basic fin-control loop is otherwise correct.

canonical_answers.title: Active Fin Stabilisers — Preference, Suitability & Partial Damping
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Fins vs passive tanks in large vessels.** Fin lift is proportional to the square of speed and to fin area; a large, fast vessel has ample speed and hull length for fins of adequate area, developing a large stabilising moment for comparatively little weight and space. A passive tank would need an enormous water mass to match this, costing space, deadweight and raising the centre of gravity.

**(b) Fins for passenger and fast cargo ships.** These ships operate at high, steady speeds — exactly where fins are most effective. The anticipatory response (sensing angle, velocity, acceleration) holds roll to small angles, giving passenger comfort and protecting cargo, while allowing speed to be maintained in a seaway.

**(c) Why partial rather than maximum damping.** In heavy weather, irregular waves mean the ship's roll is no longer smooth and predictable; a system driven hard for maximum correction can apply its force out of phase with the actual roll, reinforcing rather than opposing it. A ship held rigidly upright also loses its natural ability to "give" to the sea, increasing hull and fin stresses. Removing all roll forces the fins to work continuously near their stall angle, where lift becomes unpredictable. Partial damping keeps the fins in phase, lets the ship ride naturally, and avoids stall.
examiner_focus: Parts (a)-(b) are handled well. Part (c) is the specific trap: the question explicitly excludes stress on the fin stocks/activating gear as a reason, yet many candidates answer with exactly that anyway -- the correct angle is passenger/crew COMFORT (avoiding rapid or excessive correction that itself feels uncomfortable), not stresses on equipment.

canonical_answers.title: Partial vs Maximum Damping — Simplified Explanation
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
A more concise restatement of Q4(c) above, for use where the question is asked on its own.

First, in heavy weather the waves are irregular, so the roll is not a smooth, predictable motion; a system driven hard to cancel it completely can apply its corrective force out of step with the actual roll, pushing the ship the same way it is already rolling and making things worse. Second, a ship allowed to roll a little can "give" to the waves and ride them easily, whereas one held bolt upright resists the full wave force directly into the hull and fins. Third, removing all roll forces the fins to work continuously near their stall angle, where a sudden loss of lift makes them unreliable exactly when needed most. Partial damping keeps the fins in phase, lets the ship ride naturally, and keeps the fins clear of stall.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; same underlying point as Q4(c) in simplified form -- partial damping is preferred in heavy weather mainly for occupant comfort (avoiding abrupt corrective motion), independent of the equipment-stress reasoning the question sets aside.

canonical_answers.title: Rotary Vane Steering Gear — Circuit, Leak Operation, Advantages
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw the rotary vane actuator on the rudder stock with shock/relief valves either side, isolating valves, two independent 50% power units each with its own pump, motor, directional control valve (D.C.V.) and reservoir, and a common storage tank with a low-level alarm.*

**(a)** The rotary vane actuator is keyed directly to the rudder stock: a rotor with vanes turns between fixed stator vanes, oil pumped into one set of chambers turning the rudder one way, the other set turning it the other way. Each 50% power unit has its own fixed-delivery pump and reversing directional control valve; both units together give full slewing speed, either alone gives half speed.

**(b) Operation with an oil leak.** The two power units are completely independent. A low-level alarm on the affected reservoir gives early warning; the faulty unit or leaking section is isolated by closing its isolating valves, stopping further loss. The sound 50% unit continues supplying the actuator, so steering is maintained at reduced rate — the single-failure principle in action.

**(c) Advantages over four-ram gear.** Far more compact and lighter (torque applied directly to the stock, no rams/crossheads/tiller/Rapson-slide linkage); fewer moving parts and less maintenance; constant torque throughout the rudder angle (a four-ram's torque varies with angle); readily gives larger rudder angles; uses less oil; runs more smoothly and quietly.
examiner_focus: A rarely-attempted question -- low attempt numbers rather than poor answers from those who do try; the mark-earning content is showing 2 x 50% rotary-vane units with the directional control valve arrangement, and covering both the leak-tolerant redundancy and the specific advantages over four-ram gear (fewer major hydraulic joints/seals, more compact, no ram-seal leakage points along an exposed rod).

canonical_answers.title: Hydraulic Steering Gear — Couplings, Locking, Isolation, Single Failure
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a)** As per Q2(b)(i) above — vibration, pressure surges, corrosion, ageing seals, incorrect assembly, inadequate support.

**(b) Why locking and isolation are urgent.** A hydraulic failure removes the gear's ability to hold the rudder, so water forces will swing it hard over, leaving the ship both unable to steer and turning uncontrollably — a serious hazard in traffic. Locking keeps the rudder on a safe heading during repairs; rapid isolation stops continued oil loss, conserving enough for the sound unit and confining the fault.

**(c) Problems locking in heavy weather.** Wave and slamming loads are resisted entirely by the locking arrangement and rudder stock instead of being relieved by the gear, risking overstressing or damage; getting the rudder to the desired position and holding it accurately amidships is also difficult with heavy seas constantly forcing it one way and the other.

**(d) Why hydraulic locking is preferable.** Trapping oil on both sides of the rams/vanes holds the rudder on an incompressible but still slightly "giving" oil column that can absorb shock through relief/shock valves, cushioning wave loads. It is quick to apply and release from the steering gear itself. A mechanical lock (clamp/pin) applies a rigid, unyielding restraint that transmits full shock loading into the structure and takes longer to fit/remove.

**(e) Single failure concept.** As per Q2(b)(ii) above.
examiner_focus: Mostly fine, but two specific points recur: part (a) answers are too brief (stating 'vibration' alone isn't enough -- it needs the consequence spelled out, e.g. 'vibration leads to fatigue failure of the coupling'), and part (e) repeats the same single-failure-concept misconception as Q2 -- it isn't only about oil leakage, electrical continuity also has to be maintained.

canonical_answers.title: Reading a Rotary Vane Circuit Diagram (Component Identification)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
The rotary vane actuator: the stator (outer housing) is bolted to the ship's structure with fixed vanes projecting inward; the rotor, keyed directly to the rudder stock, carries the rotor vanes, dividing the housing into working chambers connected by oil ports.

Two 50% power units, each with its own motor-driven pump: both together give full slewing rate, either alone gives half speed. Direction valves (reversing directional control valves), one per pump, set whether the rudder goes port or starboard. An isolation valve between the actuator and power units allows a failed section to be shut off. Shock valves near the actuator relieve sudden pressure surges from wave impact; relief valves at the pumps protect against sustained overpressure. The reservoir supplies the pumps and receives returns.

**Operation.** Each pump delivers through its direction valve into one set of chambers, turning the rudder stock; displaced oil from the opposite chambers returns to tank. Reversing the direction valve reverses the rudder. The isolation valve satisfies the single-failure principle by letting a defective branch be shut off.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; as a component-identification question against a supplied rotary-vane circuit diagram, the expected answer names each stator/rotor vane, the directional control valves, the relief/anti-cavitation valves and the changeover arrangement, tying each to its role in the circuit shown.

canonical_answers.title: Rotary Vane — Continued Operation on a Leak (Standalone)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown: Same content as Q6(b) above: the two independent 50% units, low-level alarm detection, isolation of the leaking section, and continued operation at reduced rate on the sound unit — with shock valves still protecting the actuator throughout.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; this is the same 'continued operation on a leak' content as Q6/Q14's part (b) -- the key point is that a rotary-vane system built as 2 x 50% units can isolate the leaking unit and continue steering (at reduced torque/rate) on the remaining 50% unit alone.

canonical_answers.title: Four-Ram Steering Gear — Five Ram/Valve Combinations
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw four rams on the tiller (upper pair 1&2, lower pair 3&4) with isolating valves V1-V4, pair bypass valves BU/BL, two reversible variable-delivery pumps P1/P2 each with a pump isolating valve IP1/IP2, and a make-up tank with low-level alarm.*

Pressurising the left cylinders (1&3) turns the rudder one way, the right cylinders (2&4) the other. The five combinations:

**1.** P1+P2, all four rams, all valves open, bypasses closed — full speed + full torque (normal seagoing, 35–30° in 28s).
**2.** P1 only, all four rams — full torque, half speed (heavy weather / P2 down).
**3.** P2 only, all four rams — full torque, half speed (P1 isolated for maintenance).
**4.** P1+P2, upper pair only (V3/V4 closed, BL open) — full speed, half torque (light steering, fine weather).
**5.** P1 only, upper pair only — half speed, half torque (economy/standby).

In combinations 4 and 5 the lower pair is shut off and its bypass opened so it floats freely with the tiller rather than being hydraulically locked — the same valving lets a defective pump or leaking cylinder be isolated while steering continues on the remaining rams.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the five combinations for a four-ram gear typically cover all four rams together, then various pairs/singles isolated via the valve arrangement -- each combination needs its specific ram(s) and valve state identified, not just the full-power configuration.

canonical_answers.title: Four-Ram Steering Gear — Combinations 6 and 7 (Lower Pair)
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**6.** P1+P2, lower pair only (V1/V2 closed, BU open) — full speed, half torque (light steering in fine weather, on the lower pair).
**7.** P1 only, lower pair only — half speed, half torque (economy/standby, on the lower pair).

Here the upper pair is isolated and its bypass opened so it travels freely with the tiller — these two combinations simply transfer the half-torque modes onto the other pair, useful when a cylinder or valve in the upper pair is defective.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; this is a continuation/companion entry tabulating combinations 6 and 7 of the four-ram circuit (with V1/V2 closed and the bypass valve open) alongside the main Q10 answer -- treat it as an extension of the same circuit, not a standalone system.

canonical_answers.title: Sluggish Steering Gear After Heavy Weather
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Five possible reasons**
Air in the hydraulic system — heavy motion plus low oil level draws in air, giving spongy, slow response.
Low oil level/loss of oil — a leak started by storm shock loading.
Relief or shock valve passing — repeated pressure surges leave it not reseating, bypassing pump delivery.
Worn or damaged pump — sustained high-pressure operation during the storm wears internals, reducing delivery.
Increased mechanical resistance or contaminated/wrong-grade oil — damage to rudder/stock bearings, a choked filter, or thickened oil.

**(b) Corrective actions at sea**
Bring the second power unit into operation to restore full delivery.
Check and replenish the oil from the storage tank.
Vent (bleed) the system at the highest points, working the gear hard-over to hard-over to expel air.
Find and isolate any leak; check and reseat/reset any passing relief/shock valves.
Clean filters, isolate any suspect pump/cylinder and continue on the sound unit; reduce speed to lower rudder load, and steer using local control if necessary while proceeding to the nearest port.
examiner_focus: Well attempted overall, but the question's own framing (sluggish steering AFTER heavy weather) is a strong steer toward mechanical/structural causes -- worn ram bearings, bent rams, damaged relief/safety devices from shock loading -- rather than routine faults like dirty filters or low oil level, which several candidates defaulted to instead. Part (b) (corrective action at sea) is also weakly answered.

canonical_answers.title: Four-Ram with Automatic Isolation Within 45 Seconds
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
*Sketch instructions: draw a four-ram circuit split into two independent halves, each with its own 50% pump, sump and directional control valve, a split-lower-section header (replenishing) tank with level switches, a control valve, and an automatic isolating valve in the cross-connection between the halves.*

**(b) How automatic isolation is achieved.** Each half has its own supply and level switches in its sump (and the split header tank). If a leak develops in one half, its level switch trips, signalling the control valve, which pilots the isolating valve in the cross-connection to close automatically — separating the leaking half from the sound half and confining the fault. The bypass valve on the affected side opens so its cylinders float freely with the tiller. Because detection and response are entirely automatic, the changeover completes well within 45 seconds, and the remaining sound 50% unit continues supplying its pair of rams — satisfying the single-failure concept.
examiner_focus: The recurring sketch error is drawing a 2 x 100% torque system (one pump driving two rams as the working set, the second pump/pair as pure standby) when the question specifically asks for 2 x 50% torque units, where both halves work simultaneously under normal conditions and either half alone can still steer the vessel if isolated.

canonical_answers.title: Rotary Vane (from Supplied Sketch) — Leak Operation & Advantages
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
Same underlying content as Q6 above, worked from a supplied circuit sketch showing two 50% units, shock valves, an isolation valve, direction valves and relief valves.

The two 50% units are independent, each with its own pump, motor, direction valve and relief valve, drawing from its own side of the sump; the actuator is served through the isolation valve. On a leak, falling oil level is detected and the isolation valve closed, shutting off the leaking section. The remaining unit continues supplying the actuator at reduced rate, with the shock valves still protecting it against pressure surges.
examiner_focus: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; same content and traps as Q6 -- show the 2 x 50% unit arrangement with directional control valves, and give the rotary-vane-vs-four-ram advantages (compactness, fewer seals/joints, no long exposed ram rods).
